title: Everyday Chemical Foundations III: Formulas, Polyatomic Ions & Naming Logic
summary: Part 3 of the Everyday Chemical Foundations series: a warm, relaxed 100-question journey that turns mysterious ingredient labels into clear, readable chemical stories—with zero quantum-orbital jargon or stoichiometry math. Building gently on Parts I and II, learners master subscripts, parentheses, hydration dots, polyatomic ion 'team packages,' Roman numeral charge signposts, '-ate'/'-ite' oxyanion patterns, Greek covalent prefixes, and everyday acid names across kitchen pantries, pharmacy shelves, garden soils, and human physiology—bridging seamlessly to Part IV.

Ammonium, Hydroxide & Acetate—introducing polyatomic ions as sturdy covalently bonded molecular 'team packages' carrying one shared overall charge in water, warmly befriending ammonium ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$, our key positive polyatomic ion in baking/smelling salts and soil nitrogen), hydroxide ($$\text{OH}^-$$ in soap-making lye and milk of magnesia $$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$, gently demystifying why parentheses wrap multi-atom ion groups whenever more than one package is needed!), and organic acetate ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$ from culinary vinegar and reusable hand-warmer packs); (5) Bicarbonate & Carbonate in Kitchens, Shells and Blood—meeting carbonate ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$ in seashells, limestone, Tums antacids $$\text{CaCO}_3$$, and washing soda $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$$) alongside its proton-carrying sibling bicarbonate / hydrogen carbonate ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$ in pantry baking soda $$\text{NaHCO}_3$$ and human blood plasma's primary acid–base buffer); (6) Sulfate, Nitrate & Phosphate in Baths, Plants and DNA—befriending sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$ in plaster gypsum and soothing Epsom salt, gently explaining hydrate dot notation in $$\text{MgSO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ as cozy water molecules tucked into a dry crystal), nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$ in spinach, beets, and garden fertilizers), and phosphate ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$ plus protonated cousins $$\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$$ and $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$ building DNA backbones, cellular ATP, bone mineral $$\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$$, and plant food); sulfate $$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$ vs. wine-preserving sulfite $$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$), plus a friendly everyday glimpse of 'hypo-' and 'per-' through household bleach sodium hypochlorite ($$\text{NaClO}$$, holding $$\text{ClO}^-$$) and perchlorate ($$\text{ClO}_4^-$$); sections.title: 1. Reading Chemical Formulas from Scratch: Subscripts, Molecules & Crystal Units
sections.summary: Demystifies chemical formulas as compact recipes that tell us which elements are present and in what exact atomic ratio. Across five unhurried chunks, learners read element symbols alongside right-hand subscripts (including why an unwritten '1' is always implied in water $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ and carbon dioxide $$\text{CO}_2$$), contrast self-contained covalent molecules like water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) and blood sugar glucose ($$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$$) with vast repeating 3D ionic crystal lattices, and see why ionic solids like table salt ($$\text{NaCl}$$) and fluorite toothpaste mineral ($$\text{CaF}_2$$) are written as simplest lowest-whole-number formula units rather than giant multi-million-ion clusters.

chunks.title: The Pantry Recipe Code: Element Symbols & Right-Hand Subscripts
chunks.content_markdown:
Pick up a bottle of sparkling water, a box of table salt, or a packet of sports-drink powder, and you are holding substances built from countable atoms in exact, unchanging ratios. In Part I, we saw Proust and Dalton discover that every pure compound locks its elements into fixed whole-number proportions. To write those proportions without a paragraph of prose, chemists use a **chemical formula**: a compact shorthand combining element symbols with small lower-right numbers called **subscripts**.

Each **subscript** applies *only* to the element symbol sitting immediately to its left, telling you how many atoms of that element belong to the recipe. In sparkling water's dissolved gas, carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$), the subscript $$2$$ sits directly to the right of oxygen ($$\text{O}$$), meaning two oxygen atoms team up with carbon. Notice how a chemical formula reads just like a kitchen recipe card: the capitalized letters name the ingredients, and the subscripts give the exact headcount of each atom.

questions.prompt: In a standard chemical formula, what does a small lower-right subscript number directly indicate?
choices: The atomic number of the element located immediately to its left
The count of atoms of the element located immediately to its left
The total number of valence electrons shared across the entire compound
The electrical charge carried by the first element written in the formula
questions.explanation: A right-hand subscript tells you the exact count of atoms of the single element symbol sitting immediately to its left.

questions.prompt: Rust contains iron and oxygen combined in the formula $$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$$. How many iron and oxygen atoms are represented in this recipe?
choices: Three iron atoms combined with two oxygen atoms
Two iron atoms combined with two oxygen atoms
Two iron atoms combined with three oxygen atoms
Five iron atoms combined with three oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: In $$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$$, the subscript $$2$$ belongs to iron ($$\text{Fe}$$) and the subscript $$3$$ belongs to oxygen ($$\text{O}$$), giving two iron atoms for every three oxygen atoms.

chunks.title: Why the Number '1' Is Invisible: Reading $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ and $$\text{CO}_2$$
chunks.content_markdown:
When people first look closely at the formula for water, $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$, a natural question pops up: if the $$2$$ sits to the right of hydrogen ($$\text{H}$$), why is there no number at all to the right of oxygen ($$\text{O}$$)? The answer is a simple typographic habit. Just as telling a baker "bring me an apple" already means *one* apple, writing an element symbol like $$\text{O}$$ or $$\text{C}$$ in a formula already guarantees that at least one atom of that element is present.

Chemists therefore omit the subscript $$1$$ completely. Writing $$\text{H}_2\text{O}_1$$ or $$\text{C}_1\text{O}_2$$ isn't mathematically wrong, just cluttered—like writing $$1x^1$$ in algebra. So whenever you see an element symbol with no subscript to its right, mentally read an invisible $$1$$. In $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$, two hydrogen atoms pair with *one* oxygen atom (three atoms total); in $$\text{CO}_2$$, *one* carbon atom pairs with two oxygen atoms.

questions.prompt: Why do chemists write the formula for water as $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ rather than $$\text{H}_2\text{O}_1$$?
choices: Because oxygen in liquid water carries no protons in its outer shell
Because writing the element symbol itself already implies a count of one
Because the subscript 2 applies equally to both hydrogen and oxygen
Because oxygen atoms in water constantly swap places with hydrogen atoms
questions.explanation: Writing an element symbol in a formula already indicates that one atom of that element is present, so a subscript of 1 is omitted to keep formulas clean.

questions.prompt: Baking soda has the chemical formula $$\text{NaHCO}_3$$. Counting every implied '1', how many total atoms are shown in this single formula?
choices: Three total atoms across the four elements
Four total atoms across the four elements
Five total atoms across the four elements
Six total atoms across the four elements
questions.explanation: In $$\text{NaHCO}_3$$, sodium ($$\text{Na}$$), hydrogen ($$\text{H}$$), and carbon ($$\text{C}$$) each have an implied subscript of $$1$$, and oxygen ($$\text{O}$$) has a subscript of $$3$$, totaling $$1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 6$$ atoms.

chunks.title: Self-Contained Packets: Discrete Molecules and Molecular Formulas
chunks.content_markdown:
What does a chemical formula actually look like if you could zoom in to the atomic scale? That depends on whether the atoms are sharing outer valence electrons or trading them to form ions. When nonmetal atoms such as hydrogen, carbon, and oxygen share valence electrons with one another, they lock together into a self-contained, independent cluster called a **discrete molecule**. Each molecule is a true individual island: in a glass of water, trillions of separate $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ trios tumble past one another without merging into a single giant super-atom.

For any substance made of discrete molecules, its **molecular formula** reports the exact, literal inventory of atoms inside one single molecular packet. A single molecule of blood sugar—glucose, $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$$—actually travels through your bloodstream as a tidy 24-atom bundle containing exactly six carbon atoms, twelve hydrogen atoms, and six oxygen atoms.

questions.prompt: What does the molecular formula for glucose, $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$$, tell us about a single dissolved glucose particle in your bloodstream?
choices: It is an independent 24-atom packet with 6 carbons, 12 hydrogens, and 6 oxygens
It is an endless crystal lattice where carbon and oxygen alternate in a 1:2:1 grid
It splits apart into 6 separate carbon ions and 12 separate hydrogen ions in water
It contains 6 smaller water molecules loosely glued onto a pure carbon core
questions.explanation: Because glucose is a covalent molecular substance, its molecular formula $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$$ gives the exact headcount of atoms bonded inside each self-contained 24-atom molecule.

questions.prompt: Why don't chemists simplify the molecular formula of glucose from $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$$ down to $$\text{CH}_2\text{O}$$ when describing the actual molecule?
choices: Because simplifying the subscripts would change the charge of the carbon atoms
Because an individual glucose molecule physically contains 24 atoms, not 4
Because subscripts in covalent formulas must always be even whole numbers
Because oxygen atoms cannot bond unless at least six of them are present
questions.explanation: A molecular formula reports the actual number of atoms inside one discrete molecule; shrinking $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$$ to $$\text{CH}_2\text{O}$$ (which is formaldehyde!) would misstate the size of the real 24-atom packet.

chunks.title: No Lonely Couples in the Salt Shaker: Ionic Lattices & Formula Units
chunks.content_markdown:
Now sprinkle a single grain of table salt ($$\text{NaCl}$$) onto your palm. It is tempting to picture that grain as a pile of tiny, separate two-atom $$\text{NaCl}$$ "molecules"—each sodium cation ($$\text{Na}^+$$) paired off privately with one chloride anion ($$\text{Cl}^-$$). Yet as we saw in Part II, electrostatic attraction doesn't point in just one direction! A positive $$\text{Na}^+$$ ion pulls equally on negative $$\text{Cl}^-$$ neighbors above, below, left, right, front, and back.

Instead of forming isolated pairs, billions of alternating $$\text{Na}^+$$ and $$\text{Cl}^-$$ ions stack into a continuous three-dimensional checkerboard called an **ionic crystal lattice**. Because the entire salt grain is one uninterrupted network, we can't write a formula counting every ion in the speck—every grain is a different size! Instead, chemists write the **formula unit**: the simplest, lowest whole-number ratio of ions in the lattice. For table salt, that $$1:1$$ repeating tile is $$\text{NaCl}$$.

questions.prompt: Why is it scientifically inaccurate to refer to a solid grain of table salt as a collection of isolated two-atom $$\text{NaCl}$$ molecules?
choices: Because sodium and chlorine atoms fuse their nuclei together inside solid salt
Because each ion attracts six surrounding neighbors in a continuous 3D lattice
Because solid table salt contains two chloride ions for every one sodium ion
Because table salt exists only as neutral diatomic gases until it touches water
questions.explanation: In an ionic crystal lattice, electrostatic attraction acts in all directions, so each $$\text{Na}^+$$ is surrounded by six $$\text{Cl}^-$$ neighbors (and vice versa) in a continuous 3D grid rather than isolated pairs.

questions.prompt: What does the chemical formula $$\text{NaCl}$$ represent when describing a crystal of table salt?
choices: The exact total number of ions inside one microscopic salt crystal
A discrete two-atom packet held together by shared valence electrons
The simplest 1:1 whole-number ratio of sodium to chloride ions in the lattice
The temporary pairing that forms only after the salt boils into a vapor
questions.explanation: For an ionic solid, the formula unit $$\text{NaCl}$$ states the simplest lowest-whole-number ratio ($$1:1$$) of $$\text{Na}^+$$ cations to $$\text{Cl}^-$$ anions repeating throughout the crystal lattice.

chunks.title: Reading Both Worlds Side by Side: From Fluorite to Kitchen Sugar
chunks.content_markdown:
Once you know the difference between a discrete **molecular formula** and a crystal **formula unit**, you can read both kinds of chemical shorthand with confidence—even though they look identical on paper! Take the mineral fluorite, $$\text{CaF}_2$$, the natural source of cavity-fighting fluoride. Because it pairs a metal cation ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$) with nonmetal anions ($$\text{F}^-$$), $$\text{CaF}_2$$ is a **formula unit**: it tells us that inside the continuous crystal lattice, there are exactly two fluoride ions for every one calcium ion.

Contrast that with rubbing alcohol, $$\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{O}$$, or table sugar, $$\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}$$. Built entirely of nonmetal atoms sharing electrons, these formulas describe genuine **discrete molecules** containing $$12$$ and $$45$$ atoms per packet, respectively. That raises a delicious next question: in an ionic formula unit like $$\text{NaCl}$$ or $$\text{CaF}_2$$, what decides whether the subscript is $$1$$, $$2$$, or $$3$$? In Section 2, we'll see how simple charge balance gives the answer automatically.

questions.prompt: Toothpaste mineral fluorite has the formula $$\text{CaF}_2$$. What does this formula unit tell us about the solid fluorite crystal?
choices: The crystal is built from isolated three-atom molecules floating freely apart
The continuous lattice contains two calcium ions for every one fluoride ion
The continuous lattice contains two fluoride ions for every one calcium ion
Each calcium ion shares two protons directly with a diatomic fluorine gas molecule
questions.explanation: As an ionic formula unit, $$\text{CaF}_2$$ tells us that the repeating crystal lattice contains a $$1:2$$ ratio of one calcium ion ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$) for every two fluoride ions ($$\text{F}^-$$).

questions.prompt: How can you tell at a glance that $$\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11}$$ (table sugar) describes a discrete molecule while $$\text{NaCl}$$ describes an ionic formula unit?
choices: Sugar has odd-numbered subscripts, whereas ionic formula units only contain even subscripts
Sugar dissolves in warm kitchen water, whereas ionic crystal lattices never dissolve in water
Sugar contains three different elements, whereas ionic compounds only ever contain two elements
Sugar combines nonmetals sharing electrons, whereas salt pairs a metal with a nonmetal
questions.explanation: Compounds made solely of nonmetals (like $$\text{C}$$, $$\text{H}$$, and $$\text{O}$$ in sugar) share electrons in discrete molecules, whereas a metal cation paired with a nonmetal anion ($$\text{Na}^+$$ and $$\text{Cl}^-$$) forms an ionic crystal lattice described by a formula unit.

sections.title: 2. Zero-Net-Charge Ionic Pairing & Binary '-ide' Naming
sections.summary: Explores how opposing ionic charges from Part II team up in simple whole-number ratios so that every macroscopic salt crystal is electrically neutral overall. Learners practice intuitive charge balancing without algebra—seeing why one $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ pairs with two $$\text{Cl}^-$$ ions in culinary nigari tofu coagulant ($$\text{MgCl}_2$$), why one $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ matches one $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ in masonry quicklime ($$\text{CaO}$$), and why two $$\text{Na}^+$$ ions balance one $$\text{S}^{2-}$$ in $$\text{Na}_2\text{S}$$—before mastering the clean binary ionic naming rule 'metal cation name + nonmetal root-ide' across sodium chloride ($$\text{NaCl}$$), potassium iodide in iodized salt ($$\text{KI}$$), calcium fluoride ($$\text{CaF}_2$$), and magnesium oxide ($$\text{MgO}$$).

chunks.title: Why Doesn't the Salt Shaker Shock Your Fingers? The Zero-Net-Charge Rule
chunks.content_markdown:
In Part II, we met the lively cast of ions that keep our nerves firing and muscles contracting: monovalent cations like $$\text{Na}^+$$ and $$\text{K}^+$$, divalent cations like $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ and $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$, and negative anions like $$\text{Cl}^-$$, $$\text{F}^-$$, and $$\text{O}^{2-}$$. That raises a fun everyday puzzle: if a spoonful of salt is packed from edge to edge with trillions of electrically charged ions, why doesn't touching it give your fingertips a static zap?

The reason is **electrical neutrality**, often called the **zero-net-charge rule**. Electrostatic attraction and repulsion are so extraordinarily strong that you can never scoop up a jar of pure $$\text{Na}^+$$ ions by themselves—like charges would violently repel one another. Instead, positive cations and negative anions always assemble in the exact whole-number ratio where Total Positive Charge plus Total Negative Charge equals zero. Note that inside the finished neutral formula (like $$\text{NaCl}$$), we drop the individual $$+$$ and $$-$$ superscripts, even though the charged ions are still right there inside the crystal.

questions.prompt: Why does a macroscopic crystal of an ionic salt carry no overall electrical charge that would shock your hand?
choices: Because cations and anions lose their protons as soon as they pack into a solid crystal
Because positive and negative ions always assemble in a ratio whose charges sum to zero
Because air moisture coats every salt crystal with an insulating skin of neutral nitrogen
Because only liquid solutions can contain ions, whereas solid crystals contain neutral atoms
questions.explanation: By the electrical neutrality (zero-net-charge) rule, cations and anions pack into a crystal lattice in the exact whole-number ratio where total positive charge completely cancels total negative charge.

questions.prompt: Why do chemists write the formula of table salt as $$\text{NaCl}$$ without showing the $$+$$ and $$-$$ signs of $$\text{Na}^+$$ and $$\text{Cl}^-$$?
choices: Because the finished formula unit represents an electrically neutral overall combination
Because sodium and chlorine switch from ionic bonding to covalent bonding when dry
Because chloride anions transfer their extra electrons back to sodium inside the shaker
Because superscript charges are only allowed when writing radioactive isotope symbols
questions.explanation: Standard chemical formulas for ionic compounds omit the individual ion superscripts because the complete formula unit has a net electrical charge of zero.

chunks.title: Balancing the Seesaw: Why Tofu Coagulant Is $$\text{MgCl}_2$$
chunks.content_markdown:
Once you know the zero-net-charge rule, you never have to memorize ionic subscripts—you can work them out on a mental seesaw in seconds. Suppose you are making fresh silken tofu in a kitchen pot by stirring *nigari*—natural sea-salt bittern rich in magnesium and chloride ions—into warm soy milk. What is the chemical formula of this magnesium-and-chlorine salt?

From Part II, magnesium sits in the divalent alkaline earth family, so each magnesium cation carries a double positive charge: $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$. Chlorine sits in the halogen family one step short of a full valence skin, so each chloride anion carries a single negative charge: $$\text{Cl}^-$$. If one $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ ion ($$+2$$) teams up with just one $$\text{Cl}^-$$ ion ($$-1$$), the net charge is still $$+1$$—the seesaw isn't level! To balance a single $$+2$$ magnesium ion to zero, we need *two* $$-1$$ chloride ions: $$(+2) + 2(-1) = 0$$. Writing the metal cation first and the anion second gives $$\text{MgCl}_2$$.

questions.prompt: Why does the formula unit for magnesium chloride (used as culinary tofu coagulant) require a subscript 2 on chlorine in $$\text{MgCl}_2$$?
choices: Because chlorine always travels as a covalently bonded diatomic gas inside ionic crystals
Because two $$-1$$ chloride anions are needed to balance the $$+2$$ charge of one $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ cation
Because magnesium has two inner electron shells that each trap a neutral chlorine atom
Because one magnesium ion donates two protons directly to the nucleus of each chloride ion
questions.explanation: Each magnesium cation carries a $$+2$$ charge ($$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$) while each chloride anion carries a $$-1$$ charge ($$\text{Cl}^-$$), so two $$\text{Cl}^-$$ ions are needed to reach a zero net charge: $$(+2) + 2(-1) = 0$$.

questions.prompt: If potassium forms a monovalent cation ($$\text{K}^+$$) and oxygen forms a divalent oxide anion ($$\text{O}^{2-}$$), what is the neutral formula unit when they combine?
choices: $$\text{KO}$$
$$\text{KO}_2$$
$$\text{K}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{K}_2\text{O}_2$$
questions.explanation: It takes two $$+1$$ potassium cations ($$\text{K}^+$$) to balance one $$-2$$ oxide anion ($$\text{O}^{2-}$$) so that $$2(+1) + (-2) = 0$$, giving the formula unit $$\text{K}_2\text{O}$$.

chunks.title: Matching Double Charges and the 2-to-3 Handshake: $$\text{CaO}$$ and $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$$
chunks.content_markdown:
What happens when *both* the metal cation and the nonmetal anion carry double charges? Consider traditional masonry quicklime—also used since antiquity in nixtamalizing corn for tortillas—which pairs divalent calcium cations ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$) with divalent oxide anions ($$\text{O}^{2-}$$). Since one $$+2$$ ion already balances one $$-2$$ ion on the first try, $$(+2) + (-2) = 0$$, their simplest whole-number ratio is $$1:1$$. We write the formula unit simply as $$\text{CaO}$$, never $$\text{Ca}_2\text{O}_2$$.

And what if a $$+3$$ ion meets a $$-2$$ ion, as in sapphire and protective cookware coatings made of aluminum ($$\text{Al}^{3+}$$) and oxide ($$\text{O}^{2-}$$)? Look for the smallest common target where $$+3$$ charges and $$-2$$ charges meet: six! Two $$\text{Al}^{3+}$$ ions supply $$2 \times (+3) = +6$$, and three $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ ions supply $$3 \times (-2) = -6$$. Together, $$+6$$ and $$-6$$ cancel to zero, giving the rock-solid formula unit $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$$.

questions.prompt: Calcium forms a $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ cation and oxygen forms an $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ anion. Why is the formula unit of quicklime written as $$\text{CaO}$$ rather than $$\text{Ca}_2\text{O}_2$$?
choices: Because calcium and oxygen lose one charge unit each through friction when heated
Because one $$+2$$ cation and one $$-2$$ anion already balance to zero in a 1:1 ratio
Because chemical formulas are never allowed to display the same subscript twice
Because oxygen cannot form a crystal lattice if more than one atom is present
questions.explanation: A formula unit always uses the simplest lowest-whole-number ratio of ions; since one $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ ($$+2$$) and one $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ ($$-2$$) already sum to zero, the $$1:1$$ formula unit is $$\text{CaO}$$.

questions.prompt: Aluminum forms $$\text{Al}^{3+}$$ cations and sulfur forms divalent sulfide anions, $$\text{S}^{2-}$$. What is the electrically neutral formula unit when they combine?
choices: $$\text{AlS}$$
$$\text{Al}_3\text{S}_2$$
$$\text{Al}_2\text{S}_3$$
$$\text{Al}_6\text{S}_6$$
questions.explanation: Two $$\text{Al}^{3+}$$ cations provide $$+6$$ total charge and three $$\text{S}^{2-}$$ anions provide $$-6$$ total charge, balancing at $$0$$ in the formula unit $$\text{Al}_2\text{S}_3$$.

chunks.title: Two Elements, One Clean Name: The Binary '-ide' Rule
chunks.content_markdown:
Now that you can build neutral ionic formulas, how do you read their names aloud on an ingredient label? Whenever an ionic salt is made of just two elements—one metal and one nonmetal—chemists call it a **binary ionic compound** (*binary* simply means "two-part"). Naming a binary ionic compound with a fixed-charge metal follows one remarkably clean rule:

1. **First word**: Write the full, unchanged English name of the metal cation (such as *sodium*, *potassium*, *magnesium*, or *calcium*).
2. **Second word**: Take the root of the single-atom (**monatomic**, from *mono-* meaning "one") nonmetal anion and replace its ending with the **monatomic anion `-ide` suffix**.

Thus chlorine becomes **chloride**, fluorine becomes **fluoride**, iodine becomes **iodide**, oxygen becomes **oxide**, sulfur becomes **sulfide**, and nitrogen becomes **nitride**. Put them together and $$\text{KI}$$—the thyroid-protecting nutrient added to iodized table salt—is simply **potassium iodide**!

questions.prompt: When a single nonmetal element like oxygen or sulfur gains electrons to form a simple monatomic anion, how does its name change in a binary ionic compound?
choices: Its name stays completely unchanged and is placed before the metal cation's name
Its root name takes the prefix 'mono-' and keeps its original element ending
Its root name takes the suffix '-ate' to show that it has a full valence shell
Its root name takes the suffix '-ide' and is placed after the metal cation's name
questions.explanation: In a binary ionic compound, the metal cation keeps its full element name first, and the single-element (monatomic) nonmetal anion takes the suffix '-ide' second (e.g., oxide, sulfide, chloride).

questions.prompt: Iodized kitchen salt contains a tiny amount of $$\text{KI}$$ to support healthy thyroid hormone production. What is the systematic chemical name of $$\text{KI}$$?
choices: Potassium iodine
Kalium moniodide
Iodide potassium
Potassium iodide
questions.explanation: $$\text{K}$$ is the metal cation potassium, and $$\text{I}^-$$ is the monatomic anion of iodine, whose ending changes to '-ide' to give potassium iodide.

chunks.title: Why isn't $$\text{CaF}_2$$ Called 'Calcium Difluoride'? Trusting Fixed Charges
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is a subtle twist that trips up almost everyone at first. If toothpaste mineral $$\text{CaF}_2$$ contains two fluoride ions, why do chemists call it simply **calcium fluoride** rather than "calcium difluoride"? Why don't we mention the subscript $$2$$ in the name?

The secret is that main-group metals like sodium ($$\text{Na}^+$$), potassium ($$\text{K}^+$$), magnesium ($$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$), calcium ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$), and aluminum ($$\text{Al}^{3+}$$) are **fixed-charge** cations: in everyday compounds, calcium *only* ever forms $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$, and fluoride *only* ever forms $$\text{F}^-$$. Because there is only one possible way for $$+2$$ and $$-1$$ to balance to zero, saying "calcium fluoride" already locks the formula into $$\text{CaF}_2$$ automatically! Adding "di-" would be redundant—like calling a bicycle a "two-wheeled bicycle." But what happens when we meet an everyday metal like iron or copper that *can* form more than one charge? That brings us straight to Section 3.

questions.prompt: Why is the ionic compound $$\text{MgCl}_2$$ named simply 'magnesium chloride' rather than 'magnesium dichloride'?
choices: Because the two chloride ions fuse into a single particle once dissolved in water
Because fixed-charge $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ and $$\text{Cl}^-$$ can only balance to zero in a 1:2 ratio
Because subscripts larger than 1 are ignored whenever a compound contains a halogen
Because the second chloride ion is an uncharged isotope that does not affect the name
questions.explanation: Since magnesium always forms $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ and chloride always forms $$\text{Cl}^-$$, a $$1:2$$ ratio is the only electrically neutral combination possible, making a numerical prefix unnecessary.

questions.prompt: A refractory ceramic brick is made of pure magnesium oxide. Given that magnesium forms $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ and oxide is $$\text{O}^{2-}$$, what is its chemical formula?
choices: $$\text{MgO}$$
$$\text{MgO}_2$$
$$\text{Mg}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{Mg}_2\text{O}_3$$
questions.explanation: Because magnesium is $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ ($$+2$$) and oxide is $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ ($$-2$$), they balance in a $$1:1$$ ratio, giving the formula unit $$\text{MgO}$$.

sections.title: 3. Variable-Charge Metals & Roman Numeral Signposts
sections.summary: Introduces everyday transition and post-transition metals that can stably shed different numbers of electrons depending on their chemical environment, explained cleanly without $$d$$-orbital or quantum-number formalism. Learners discover why a Roman numeral in parentheses—the Stock system signpost—is essential to tell apart gentle oxygen-carrying iron(II) ($$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ in hemoglobin and ferrous supplements like $$\text{FeCl}_2$$) from fully oxidized iron(III) ($$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$ in flaky red-brown rust, iron(III) oxide $$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$$), as well as copper(I) oxide ($$\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$$) vs. blue-green patina copper(II) ions ($$\text{Cu}^{2+}$$ in $$\text{CuO}$$), while recognizing why fixed-charge main-group metals like $$\text{Na}^+$$, $$\text{K}^+$$, $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$, and $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ never use Roman numerals.

chunks.title: The Tale of Two Irons: Why 'Iron Chloride' Isn't Specific Enough
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine walking into a pharmacy or chemical supply room and asking for a bottle of "iron chloride." The pharmacist would immediately pause and ask, "Which one?" On the shelf sit two completely different crystalline solids made *only* of iron and chlorine: pale green $$\text{FeCl}_2$$ and golden-brown $$\text{FeCl}_3$$. Both are genuine binary ionic salts of iron and chloride, yet they have different colors, different solubilities, and different jobs inside the human body.

Why can iron form two different chlorides when calcium only ever forms $$\text{CaCl}_2$$? Unlike main-group metals in the left-hand columns of the periodic table—whose outer valence skins always shed a single fixed number of electrons—many everyday metals across the middle of the table (such as iron, copper, tin, and lead) are **variable-charge metals** (also called **multivalent cations**). Depending on how strongly their reaction partners pull on electrons, these metals can stably lose two, three, or sometimes one electron to form distinct cations.

questions.prompt: Why is the name 'iron chloride' ambiguous on a chemical or pharmacy label, whereas 'calcium chloride' is completely clear?
choices: Because chlorine forms several different negative charges when bonded to iron
Because iron can stably form more than one positive ion charge, whereas calcium is always $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$
Because iron chloride is a covalent gas that changes its formula with room temperature
Because calcium chloride contains oxygen atoms that lock its ratio in place
questions.explanation: Iron is a variable-charge (multivalent) metal that commonly forms both $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ and $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$ cations, yielding two distinct compounds ($$\text{FeCl}_2$$ and $$\text{FeCl}_3$$), whereas calcium only ever forms $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when chemists describe a metal like copper or iron as a 'variable-charge metal' (or multivalent cation)?
choices: The metal atom constantly flips between positive and negative charges every second
The metal can stably lose different numbers of electrons in different compounds
The metal has an unstable radioactive nucleus that changes its proton count
The metal can only bond with noble gases that carry variable valence shells
questions.explanation: A variable-charge metal can stably shed different whole numbers of electrons depending on its chemical environment, forming cations with different positive charges (such as $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ vs. $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$).

chunks.title: The Roman Numeral Signpost: What the Stock System Actually Says
chunks.content_markdown:
To remove all guesswork when naming variable-charge metals, the German chemist Alfred Stock introduced a wonderfully direct signpost in 1919 known as the **Stock system**: right after the metal's English name, we write a **Roman numeral in parentheses**—such as $$\text{(I)}$$, $$\text{(II)}$$, $$\text{(III)}$$, or $$\text{(IV)}$$—with no space before the opening parenthesis.

Here is the single most important rule to remember in all of chemical naming: **the Roman numeral states the positive charge on one metal ion—NEVER the subscript count of metal atoms in the formula!**
- **Iron(II)** means each iron cation carries a $$+2$$ charge ($$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$).
- **Iron(III)** means each iron cation carries a $$+3$$ charge ($$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$).
- **Copper(I)** means $$\text{Cu}^+$$, while **copper(II)** means $$\text{Cu}^{2+}$$.

So pale green $$\text{FeCl}_2$$ (containing $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$) is **iron(II) chloride**, and golden-brown $$\text{FeCl}_3$$ (containing $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$) is **iron(III) chloride**.

questions.prompt: In a Stock-system chemical name such as 'iron(III) oxide' or 'copper(II) chloride', what does the Roman numeral inside the parentheses state?
choices: The positive electrical charge carried by each individual metal cation
The subscript number written directly to the right of the metal symbol
The total number of nonmetal anions attached to the entire crystal lattice
The row of the periodic table in which the metal element is located
questions.explanation: In the Stock system, the Roman numeral in parentheses always states the positive charge of one metal cation (e.g., iron(III) means $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$), never the subscript count of atoms.

questions.prompt: Anti-cavity toothpastes often use tin(II) fluoride to strengthen tooth enamel. Since fluoride is $$\text{F}^-$$ and tin has the symbol $$\text{Sn}$$, what is its neutral formula?
choices: $$\text{Sn}_2\text{F}$$
$$\text{Sn}_2\text{F}_2$$
$$\text{SnF}$$
$$\text{SnF}_2$$
questions.explanation: Tin(II) tells us the cation is $$\text{Sn}^{2+}$$. Balancing one $$+2$$ tin cation requires two $$-1$$ fluoride anions ($$\text{F}^-$$), giving the formula unit $$\text{SnF}_2$$.

chunks.title: Blood vs. Rust: Ferrous Iron(II) and Ferric Iron(III) in Daily Life
chunks.content_markdown:
That single charge difference between $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ and $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$ is literally a matter of life and breath. Inside the hemoglobin proteins of your red blood cells sits an **iron(II)** ion, $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$. Only in this $$+2$$ state can hemoglobin reversibly cradle an oxygen molecule ($$\text{O}_2$$) in your lungs and release it gently to your brain and muscles. On nutrition and supplement labels, you will often spot the older Latin-rooted nickname **ferrous** for iron(II) ($$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$) and **ferric** for iron(III) ($$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$)—which is why doctors prescribe *ferrous* supplements, since your gut absorbs $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ far more easily than $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$!

Leave an iron skillet out in damp air, however, and oxygen pulls a third electron away from the metal, turning $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ into **iron(III)**, $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$. Paired with oxide anions ($$\text{O}^{2-}$$), two $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$ ions ($$+6$$ total) balance three $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ ions ($$-6$$ total) to form flaky red-brown rust: **iron(III) oxide**, $$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$$.

questions.prompt: Flaky red-brown rust has the chemical formula $$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$$. Given that each oxide ion carries a $$-2$$ charge ($$\text{O}^{2-}$$), what is the correct Stock name for $$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$$?
choices: Iron(II) oxide, because the subscript on iron is 2
Iron(III) oxide, because each iron ion carries a +3 charge
Iron(VI) oxide, because the total positive charge in the unit is +6
Diiron trioxide, because iron and oxygen share electrons as gases
questions.explanation: Three $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ ions carry a total charge of $$-6$$, so the two iron ions must together supply $$+6$$, meaning each iron cation is $$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$—making $$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$$ iron(III) oxide.

questions.prompt: When an over-the-counter prenatal vitamin lists 'ferrous' iron on its nutrition panel, which specific ion is inside the tablet?
choices: Uncharged elemental iron metal filings ($$\text{Fe}$$)
Iron(I) cations carrying a single positive charge ($$\text{Fe}^+$$)
Iron(II) cations carrying a double positive charge ($$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$)
Iron(III) cations carrying a triple positive charge ($$\text{Fe}^{3+}$$)
questions.explanation: The traditional nickname 'ferrous' refers to iron(II) ($$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$), the form of iron used by hemoglobin to carry oxygen and most readily absorbed in the human digestive tract.

chunks.title: Reverse-Engineering the Charge: Copper(I) vs. Copper(II) Patinas
chunks.content_markdown:
Watch an old copper penny or a historic bronze roof weather over the years, and you are watching copper step through two different ionic charges. When bright copper metal first reacts gently with oxygen, it forms a warm brick-red layer of $$\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$$. With longer exposure to air and rain, it darkens into $$\text{CuO}$$ and eventually into the famous blue-green copper(II) patina of the Statue of Liberty.

Notice how easily you can reverse-engineer the Roman numeral from a formula like $$\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$$ or $$\text{CuO}$$—and avoid the classic trap of reading the metal's subscript! Start with the partner you know for sure: oxide is *always* $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ ($$-2$$).
- In $$\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$$, a single $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ ($$-2$$) is balanced by *two* copper ions, so each copper ion carries only a $$+1$$ charge ($$\text{Cu}^+$$). Therefore $$\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$$ is **copper(I) oxide**!
- In $$\text{CuO}$$, one $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ ($$-2$$) is balanced by *one* copper ion, so that copper ion must be $$\text{Cu}^{2+}$$—making $$\text{CuO}$$ **copper(II) oxide**.

questions.prompt: Brick-red cuprite mineral has the formula $$\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$$. Since oxide is $$\text{O}^{2-}$$, why is $$\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$$ named 'copper(I) oxide' even though there is a subscript 2 on copper?
choices: Because the Roman numeral (I) states that each of the two copper ions has a +1 charge
Because the Roman numeral (I) counts the single oxygen ion at the end of the formula
Because one of the two copper atoms in $$\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$$ is completely uncharged
Because copper always loses half of its charge when exposed to indoor air
questions.explanation: To balance one $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ ion ($$-2$$), the two copper ions in $$\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$$ must split a $$+2$$ total charge, giving $$+1$$ per ion ($$\text{Cu}^+$$)—which is what copper(I) signifies.

questions.prompt: Black tenorite mineral has the formula $$\text{CuO}$$. What is its systematic Stock name, and what charge does each copper ion carry?
choices: Copper(I) oxide, containing $$\text{Cu}^+$$ ions
Copper(II) oxide, containing $$\text{Cu}^{2+}$$ ions
Copper(I) monoxide, containing neutral $$\text{Cu}$$ atoms
Copper(IV) oxide, containing $$\text{Cu}^{4+}$$ ions
questions.explanation: In $$\text{CuO}$$, one copper ion balances one $$\text{O}^{2-}$$ ion ($$-2$$), so the copper ion carries a $$+2$$ charge ($$\text{Cu}^{2+}$$) and the compound is named copper(II) oxide.

chunks.title: Knowing When NOT to Use Roman Numerals: Fixed vs. Variable Metals
chunks.content_markdown:
Once learners discover how helpful Roman numerals are for iron and copper, it is tempting to start sprinkling them everywhere—writing "sodium(I) chloride" for table salt or "calcium(II) fluoride" for toothpaste mineral. Chemists actually forbid Roman numerals on fixed-charge metals, and for a great reason: a signpost is only helpful when there is a fork in the road!

Our familiar Group 1 alkali metals ($$\text{Li}^+$$, $$\text{Na}^+$$, $$\text{K}^+$$), Group 2 alkaline earth metals ($$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$, $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$), and aluminum ($$\text{Al}^{3+}$$) never face a fork in the road—each has only one stable ionic charge in everyday compounds. Reserve Roman numerals strictly for variable-charge metals like iron, copper, tin, lead, manganese, and chromium. Up to now, every ion we have paired has been a single charged atom. What happens when a tight-knit *team* of atoms shares a single charge together? Let's meet polyatomic ions in Section 4.

questions.prompt: Why is it incorrect in standard chemical naming to write 'calcium(II) chloride' for $$\text{CaCl}_2$$ or 'sodium(I) chloride' for $$\text{NaCl}$$?
choices: Because Roman numerals are only used for radioactive elements at the bottom of the table
Because chloride ions cancel out the need for Roman numerals in any compound
Because main-group metals form covalent molecules rather than ionic crystal lattices
Because calcium and sodium only ever form one fixed ionic charge in compounds
questions.explanation: Roman numerals are used only for variable-charge metals to prevent ambiguity; since sodium is always $$\text{Na}^+$$ and calcium is always $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$, adding a Roman numeral is redundant and incorrect.

questions.prompt: Which of the following four compounds requires a Roman numeral in its systematic chemical name?
choices: $$\text{KCl}$$ (salt-substitute electrolyte)
$$\text{MgO}$$ (antacid and refractory mineral)
$$\text{FeCl}_3$$ (water-treatment coagulant)
$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$$ (sapphire and alumina ceramic)
questions.explanation: Potassium ($$\text{K}^+$$), magnesium ($$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$), and aluminum ($$\text{Al}^{3+}$$) are fixed-charge metals, whereas iron is a variable-charge metal requiring the Stock name iron(III) chloride for $$\text{FeCl}_3$$.

sections.title: 4. What Is a Polyatomic Ion? Ammonium, Hydroxide & Acetate
sections.summary: Introduces polyatomic ions as sturdy, covalently bonded clusters of atoms that travel together in water as a single 'team package' carrying one shared overall electrical charge. Learners warmly befriend three foundational everyday packages: ammonium ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$, our primary positively charged polyatomic ion found in vintage smelling salts, bakery leaveners, and rich soil nitrogen), hydroxide ($$\text{OH}^-$$, the signature alkaline ion in soap-making lye $$\text{NaOH}$$ and soothing milk of magnesia $$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$), and organic acetate ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$ from culinary vinegar and reusable sodium acetate $$\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$$ hand warmers), while demystifying why parentheses wrap a polyatomic group whenever two or more packages are needed to balance charge.

chunks.title: The Molecular Team Package: What Is a Polyatomic Ion?
chunks.content_markdown:
Up to now, every ion we have met—like $$\text{Na}^+$$, $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$, or $$\text{Cl}^-$$—has been a *monatomic* ion: a single atom carrying an electrical charge. Yet when you read the ingredient labels on baking powder, garden fertilizer, or antacid tablets, you quickly meet formulas with three or four different elements, such as $$\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$$ or $$\text{NaOH}$$. How can an ionic salt have more than two elements?

The secret is one of chemistry's friendliest inventions: the **polyatomic ion** (*poly-* means "many"). A **polyatomic ion** is a sturdy little cluster of two or more nonmetal atoms held tightly together by shared covalent bonds, which *as a whole group* has gained or lost one or more electrons to carry a single shared net charge. Think of a polyatomic ion as a five-person bobsled team: inside the sled, the teammates hold onto each other tightly with covalent grips, while the entire sled glides through water and crystal lattices as one charged unit.

questions.prompt: How does a polyatomic ion behave when an ionic salt containing it dissolves in a glass of water?
choices: Every individual atom inside the polyatomic ion breaks apart into separate monatomic ions
The covalently bonded atom cluster stays intact and travels together as one charged unit
The polyatomic ion immediately evaporates out of the water as an uncharged gas molecule
The nonmetal atoms inside the ion fuse their nuclei together to form a heavy metal cation
questions.explanation: Inside a polyatomic ion, the atoms are held together by strong covalent bonds, so the entire cluster stays intact in water and moves as a single charged package.

questions.prompt: What two types of chemical bonding coexist inside a solid crystal of a salt that contains a polyatomic ion?
choices: Covalent bonds inside the polyatomic package, and ionic attraction between opposite ions
Metallic bonds inside the polyatomic package, and nuclear bonds between opposite ions
Radioactive bonds inside the polyatomic package, and magnetic bonds between opposite ions
Only pure covalent bonds throughout the entire crystal, with no ionic charges present
questions.explanation: A polyatomic salt features covalent electron-sharing holding the atoms of the polyatomic package together, paired with electrostatic ionic attraction between positive cations and negative anions.

chunks.title: Meet Ammonium ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$): The Honorary Metal Cation in Soil & Bakeries
chunks.content_markdown:
Almost all polyatomic ions carry a negative charge, which makes our one major positively charged hero remarkably easy to remember: the **ammonium** ion, $$\text{NH}_4^+$$. Inside an ammonium ion, one nitrogen atom and four hydrogen atoms share electrons in a tight covalent cluster that has one more proton than it has electrons, giving the entire five-atom package a $$+1$$ charge.

Be careful not to confuse **ammonium** ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$, a charged cation that forms odorless crystalline salts) with *ammonia* ($$\text{NH}_3$$, the pungent uncharged gas in window cleaner). Because $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ carries the exact same $$+1$$ charge as $$\text{Na}^+$$ or $$\text{K}^+$$, it steps into ionic crystals like an "honorary alkali metal"! Pair one $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ cation with one $$\text{Cl}^-$$ anion and you get **ammonium chloride** ($$\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$$), the tangy mineral salt flavoring Nordic black licorice and feeding nitrogen-hungry garden roots.

questions.prompt: What is the key chemical difference between household ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$) and the ammonium ion ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$)?
choices: Ammonia is a solid metal cation, whereas ammonium is an uncharged noble gas
Ammonia is an uncharged 4-atom molecule, whereas ammonium is a 5-atom cation with a +1 charge
Ammonia contains four nitrogen atoms, whereas ammonium contains four oxygen atoms
Ammonia carries a -3 electrical charge, whereas ammonium carries a -4 electrical charge
questions.explanation: Ammonia ($$\text{NH}_3$$) is a neutral covalent molecule made of one nitrogen and three hydrogens, whereas ammonium ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$) has an extra $$\text{H}^+$$ attached, making it a five-atom polyatomic cation with a $$+1$$ charge.

questions.prompt: Ammonium sulfide is used in textile manufacturing and photographic toning. Since ammonium is $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ and sulfide is $$\text{S}^{2-}$$, how many ammonium packages balance one sulfide ion?
choices: One $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ package balances one $$\text{S}^{2-}$$ ion
Two $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ packages balance one $$\text{S}^{2-}$$ ion
Three $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ packages balance one $$\text{S}^{2-}$$ ion
Four $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ packages balance one $$\text{S}^{2-}$$ ion
questions.explanation: Each ammonium ion carries a $$+1$$ charge ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$) and sulfide carries a $$-2$$ charge ($$\text{S}^{2-}$$), so two $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ packages are required to reach a net charge of zero.

chunks.title: Meet Hydroxide ($$\text{OH}^-$$) & Why Milk of Magnesia Needs Parentheses
chunks.content_markdown:
Now let's meet a two-atom polyatomic anion that shows up on soap-making and pharmacy shelves everywhere: **hydroxide**, $$\text{OH}^-$$. Notice its `-ide` ending! Although `-ide` usually signals a single-element anion like chloride ($$\text{Cl}^-$$) or oxide ($$\text{O}^{2-}$$), **hydroxide** is the famous two-atom exception: one oxygen atom and one hydrogen atom covalently bonded into a single package carrying a $$-1$$ charge. Paired $$1:1$$ with $$\text{Na}^+$$, it forms **sodium hydroxide** ($$\text{NaOH}$$, traditional soap-making lye).

What happens when we pair $$-1$$ hydroxide with divalent $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ to make soothing **magnesium hydroxide** (pharmacy "milk of magnesia")? We need *two* complete $$\text{OH}^-$$ packages to balance one $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$. If we carelessly wrote $$\text{MgOH}_2$$, the subscript $$2$$ would apply only to hydrogen—meaning one oxygen and two hydrogens! To multiply the *entire* $$\text{OH}^-$$ package by two, we wrap the group in **polyatomic parentheses notation**: $$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$.

questions.prompt: Why must the formula for magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia) be written with parentheses as $$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$ rather than $$\text{MgOH}_2$$?
choices: Because without parentheses, the subscript 2 would multiply only hydrogen instead of the whole $$\text{OH}^-$$ ion
Because parentheses show that the hydroxide group is a gas trapped inside liquid magnesium
Because magnesium is a variable-charge metal that uses parentheses instead of Roman numerals
Because any chemical formula containing three different elements must always include parentheses
questions.explanation: A subscript outside parentheses multiplies every atom inside the package; writing $$\text{MgOH}_2$$ would indicate one $$\text{O}$$ and two $$\text{H}$$ atoms rather than two intact $$\text{OH}^-$$ hydroxide ions.

questions.prompt: Why does sodium hydroxide ($$\text{NaOH}$$) NOT use parentheses around the $$\text{OH}$$ group, whereas calcium hydroxide, $$\text{Ca(OH)}_2$$, does?
choices: Because sodium bonds covalently to oxygen, whereas calcium bonds only to hydrogen
Because only one $$\text{OH}^-$$ package is needed to balance $$\text{Na}^+$$, and parentheses are omitted for a count of 1
Because sodium hydroxide contains no polyatomic ions when it is stored as a dry solid
Because parentheses are only used when the metal cation comes from an even-numbered periodic row
questions.explanation: Chemists wrap a polyatomic ion in parentheses only when two or more of that package appear in the formula unit; for a single $$\text{OH}^-$$ package in $$\text{NaOH}$$, parentheses are omitted.

chunks.title: Counting Inside and Outside Parentheses: A Step-by-Step Walkthrough
chunks.content_markdown:
Reading parentheses in a chemical formula works just like the distributive property in everyday arithmetic—or like buying shrink-wrapped twin-packs at the grocery store. Every atom subscript *inside* the parentheses gets multiplied by the subscript sitting immediately *outside* the closing parenthesis.

Let's practice on two real-world examples:
- In slaked lime, **calcium hydroxide** $$\text{Ca(OH)}_2$$, there is $$1$$ calcium ion outside the parentheses, and $$2$$ complete $$\text{OH}^-$$ packages inside. Since each $$\text{OH}^-$$ package holds $$1$$ oxygen and $$1$$ hydrogen, multiplying by $$2$$ gives $$1\text{ Ca}$$, $$2\text{ O}$$, and $$2\text{ H}$$ atoms ($$5$$ atoms total).
- In the garden fertilizer **ammonium sulfide**, $$\text{(NH}_4)_2\text{S}$$, two $$+1$$ ammonium packages balance one $$-2$$ sulfide ion. Outside the parentheses sits $$1$$ sulfur atom; inside sit $$2$$ complete $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ packages, giving $$2 \times 1 = 2$$ nitrogen atoms and $$2 \times 4 = 8$$ hydrogen atoms!

questions.prompt: In one formula unit of ammonium sulfide, $$\text{(NH}_4)_2\text{S}$$, how many nitrogen atoms and how many hydrogen atoms are present?
choices: 1 nitrogen atom and 4 hydrogen atoms
2 nitrogen atoms and 4 hydrogen atoms
2 nitrogen atoms and 8 hydrogen atoms
1 nitrogen atom and 8 hydrogen atoms
questions.explanation: The subscript $$2$$ outside the parentheses multiplies everything inside the $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ package by $$2$$, giving $$2 \times 1 = 2$$ nitrogen atoms and $$2 \times 4 = 8$$ hydrogen atoms.

questions.prompt: Antacid gels sometimes contain aluminum hydroxide, $$\text{Al(OH)}_3$$. How many total atoms (counting aluminum, oxygen, and hydrogen together) are in one formula unit of $$\text{Al(OH)}_3$$?
choices: 4 total atoms
5 total atoms
7 total atoms
9 total atoms
questions.explanation: One formula unit of $$\text{Al(OH)}_3$$ contains $$1$$ aluminum atom plus $$3$$ complete $$\text{OH}^-$$ packages ($$3$$ oxygens and $$3$$ hydrogens), for $$1 + 3 + 3 = 7$$ atoms total.

chunks.title: From Salt-and-Vinegar Chips to Pocket Hand Warmers: Meet Acetate ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$)
chunks.content_markdown:
Before we leave our first group of polyatomic ions, let's meet a wonderfully tasty organic package: the **acetate** ion, written either as $$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$ or in condensed atom-total form as $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2^-$$. Both formulas describe the exact same seven-atom cluster (two carbons, three hydrogens, and two oxygens) carrying a single $$-1$$ charge. Chemists love writing $$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$ because it visually shows a three-hydrogen carbon tail ($$\text{CH}_3$$) attached to a two-oxygen charged head ($$\text{COO}^-$$) where the $$-1$$ charge lives.

Where do you meet acetate at home? Pair it with $$\text{Na}^+$$ and you get **sodium acetate** ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$$ or $$\text{NaC}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2$$)—the powdery crystal that gives "salt and vinegar" potato chips their dry tang and fills click-to-heat reusable pocket hand warmers! Notice that because acetate comes from organic chemistry, you will often see $$\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$$ written with the anion first and $$\text{Na}$$ at the right-hand tip, though its spoken name is still always **sodium acetate**.

questions.prompt: Why is the acetate ion often written as $$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$ on food and laboratory labels instead of only as $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2^-$$?
choices: Because $$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$ carries a -2 charge whereas $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2^-$$ carries a -1 charge
Because the two carbon atoms in acetate are different radioactive isotopes of carbon
Because $$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$ is a gas molecule whereas $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2^-$$ is an ionic solid
Because $$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$ visually shows how the atoms are grouped inside the 7-atom ion
questions.explanation: Both $$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$ and $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2^-$$ contain two carbons, three hydrogens, and two oxygens with a $$-1$$ charge; $$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$ simply highlights the structural grouping of the atoms.

questions.prompt: Calcium acetate is used as a food stabilizer and kidney medication. Given that calcium is $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ and acetate is $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2^-$$, what is the neutral formula of calcium acetate?
choices: $$\text{CaC}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2$$
$$\text{Ca}_2\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2$$
$$\text{Ca(C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2)_3$$
$$\text{Ca(C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2)_2$$
questions.explanation: One $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ cation ($$+2$$) requires two $$-1$$ acetate packages to reach zero net charge, wrapped in parentheses as $$\text{Ca(C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2)_2$$.

sections.title: 5. Bicarbonate & Carbonate in Kitchens, Shells and Blood
sections.summary: Follows the carbon-oxygen polyatomic family across kitchen pantries, ocean reefs, and human physiology. Learners meet divalent carbonate ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$) in seashells, pearls, agricultural limestone, chewable Tums antacid tablets (calcium carbonate, $$\text{CaCO}_3$$), and laundry washing soda (sodium carbonate, $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$$), then see how attaching a single positive hydrogen ion ($$\text{H}^+$$) transforms $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$ into monovalent bicarbonate / hydrogen carbonate ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$)—explaining both why baking soda ($$\text{NaHCO}_3$$) needs only one sodium ion and how the carbonate–bicarbonate partnership acts as the gentle acid–base buffer protecting human blood plasma.

chunks.title: The Architect of Seashells and Antacids: Meet Carbonate ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$)
chunks.content_markdown:
What do a pearly clam shell on the beach, the white chalk cliffs of Dover, a marble kitchen countertop, and a chewable peppermint Tums antacid tablet all have in common? Every single one of them is built from the exact same ionic compound: **calcium carbonate**, $$\text{CaCO}_3$$!

Inside $$\text{CaCO}_3$$ sits one of nature's most important mineral building blocks: the **carbonate ion**, $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$. A carbonate package consists of one central carbon atom covalently bonded to three surrounding oxygen atoms, carrying an overall double negative charge ($$-2$$). Because calcium is a divalent cation ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$) and carbonate is a divalent anion ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$), one $$+2$$ calcium ion balances one $$-2$$ carbonate package in a clean $$1:1$$ ratio. And because only *one* $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$ package is present in $$\text{CaCO}_3$$, no parentheses are needed—the subscript $$3$$ simply counts the three oxygens inside that single carbonate ion.

questions.prompt: Chewable Tums antacids and natural seashells are both made of calcium carbonate, $$\text{CaCO}_3$$. How many carbonate ions ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$) are in one formula unit of $$\text{CaCO}_3$$?
choices: Three separate carbonate ions, as shown by the subscript 3 on the right
One intact carbonate ion containing one carbon atom and three oxygen atoms
Two carbonate ions that each donate an oxygen atom to the calcium ion
Zero carbonate ions, because $$\text{CaCO}_3$$ is a purely covalent gas molecule
questions.explanation: In $$\text{CaCO}_3$$, the subscript $$3$$ belongs to the three oxygen atoms inside a single $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$ carbonate ion, which balances one $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ cation $$1:1$$.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't the formula for calcium carbonate, $$\text{CaCO}_3$$, require parentheses around the $$\text{CO}_3$$ group?
choices: Because carbon and oxygen are not covalently bonded to one another in carbonate
Because only one $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$ package is needed to balance one $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ cation
Because parentheses are never allowed around polyatomic ions that contain oxygen
Because calcium shares its valence electrons equally with all three oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: Since one $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ ($$+2$$) and one $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$ ($$-2$$) balance in a $$1:1$$ ratio, only one carbonate package appears in the formula unit and parentheses are omitted.

chunks.title: Adding One Proton Changes the Charge: Meet Bicarbonate ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$)
chunks.content_markdown:
Now watch what happens when a divalent **carbonate** ion ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$) floating in water meets a single positively charged hydrogen ion, $$\text{H}^+$$ (which, as we saw in Part II, is simply a bare proton!). Drawn by electrostatic attraction, that $$+1$$ hydrogen latches covalently onto one of carbonate's oxygen atoms, creating a new five-atom polyatomic package: $$\text{HCO}_3^-$$.

Chemists call this attachment of an $$\text{H}^+$$ ion **protonation**, and notice the beautiful arithmetic of the **stepwise charge shift**: when a $$-2$$ ion ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$) gains one $$+1$$ proton ($$\text{H}^+$$), its overall charge steps up by one unit from $$-2$$ to $$-1$$:
$$(-2) + (+1) = -1$$
This monovalent $$-1$$ ion ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$) has two everyday names you will see side by side on labels: its systematic name **hydrogen carbonate**, and its beloved traditional kitchen and medical name, **bicarbonate**.

questions.prompt: When a carbonate ion ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$) attaches a single positively charged hydrogen ion ($$\text{H}^+$$) to become bicarbonate ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$), why does the overall charge change from $$-2$$ to $$-1$$?
choices: Because one of the three oxygen atoms breaks off and carries away a -1 charge
Because adding a +1 hydrogen ion neutralizes one of the two negative charges on $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$
Because the carbon atom inside the package loses a proton from its atomic nucleus
Because any polyatomic ion with five total atoms must always carry a -1 charge
questions.explanation: Attaching one $$\text{H}^+$$ ($$+1$$) to a carbonate ion ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$, charge $$-2$$) shifts the net charge of the package by $$+1$$: $$(-2) + (+1) = -1$$.

questions.prompt: Which two names on food and pharmacy ingredient panels refer to the exact same polyatomic ion, $$\text{HCO}_3^-$$?
choices: Carbonate and carbide
Bicarbonate and hydrogen carbonate
Hydroxide and hydrogencarbide
Carbonite and dicarbonate
questions.explanation: Bicarbonate is the traditional common name and hydrogen carbonate is the systematic IUPAC name for the exact same monovalent ion, $$\text{HCO}_3^-$$.

chunks.title: Baking Soda vs. Washing Soda: Why $$\text{NaHCO}_3$$ and $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$$ Differ
chunks.content_markdown:
That shift in charge between **bicarbonate** ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$, charge $$-1$$) and **carbonate** ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$ , charge $$-2$$) solves a classic household mystery: what is the difference between the orange box of **baking soda** in your refrigerator and the yellow box of **washing soda** in the laundry room?

- **Baking soda** is **sodium bicarbonate** (or *sodium hydrogen carbonate*). Because the bicarbonate package ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$) carries only a $$-1$$ charge, it needs just **one** $$\text{Na}^+$$ ion to balance to zero: $$\text{NaHCO}_3$$.
- **Washing soda** is **sodium carbonate**. Because the unprotonated carbonate package ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$) carries a $$-2$$ charge, it requires **two** $$\text{Na}^+$$ ions to balance to zero: $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$$.

That single proton makes all the difference! Gentle $$\text{NaHCO}_3$$ is mild enough to brush your teeth and leaven buttermilk pancakes, whereas strongly alkaline $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$$ cuts heavy laundry grease (and is even baked from baking soda to give traditional ramen noodles their springy snap!).

questions.prompt: Why does washing soda (sodium carbonate, $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$$) contain two sodium ions per formula unit, whereas baking soda (sodium bicarbonate, $$\text{NaHCO}_3$$) contains only one?
choices: Because carbonate carries a -2 charge requiring two $$\text{Na}^+$$ ions, while bicarbonate carries a -1 charge
Because sodium switches from a +1 cation in baking soda to a +2 cation in washing soda
Because washing soda is a discrete covalent molecule that doubles all of its metal subscripts
Because the hydrogen atom in baking soda carries a -1 charge that repels extra sodium ions
questions.explanation: In $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$$, two $$\text{Na}^+$$ cations are needed to balance the $$-2$$ charge of $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$; in $$\text{NaHCO}_3$$, the attached $$\text{H}^+$$ already reduces the anion's charge to $$-1$$ ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$), requiring only one $$\text{Na}^+$$.

questions.prompt: Potassium bicarbonate is used in club soda and potassium supplements. Given that potassium is $$\text{K}^+$$ and bicarbonate is $$\text{HCO}_3^-$$, what is its chemical formula?
choices: $$\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3$$
$$\text{KHCO}_3$$
$$\text{K}_2\text{HCO}_3$$
questions.explanation: One monovalent potassium cation ($$\text{K}^+$$, charge $$+1$$) balances one monovalent bicarbonate anion ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$, charge $$-1$$) in a $$1:1$$ ratio, giving $$\text{KHCO}_3$$.

chunks.title: Temporary Hard Water & Kettle Limescale: When $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ Meets $$\text{HCO}_3^-$$
chunks.content_markdown:
Have you ever peered inside an electric tea kettle and noticed a chalky white crust lining the bottom? That everyday limescale is a live demonstration of calcium, bicarbonate, and parentheses in action. As rainwater trickles through underground limestone ($$\text{CaCO}_3$$), dissolved carbon dioxide helps convert insoluble carbonate into soluble **bicarbonate** ions ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$).

What is the chemical formula of dissolved **calcium bicarbonate** in that mineral-rich tap water? Since each calcium cation carries a $$+2$$ charge ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$) and each bicarbonate package carries only a $$-1$$ charge ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$), one calcium ion needs *two* complete bicarbonate packages to balance to zero—wrapped neatly in parentheses as $$\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2$$! When you boil the kettle, heat drives off carbon dioxide gas and turns dissolved $$\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2$$ right back into solid, chalky calcium carbonate ($$\text{CaCO}_3$$) crust.

questions.prompt: Mineral-rich tap water often contains dissolved calcium bicarbonate. Since calcium is $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ and bicarbonate is $$\text{HCO}_3^-$$, what is the correct formula for calcium bicarbonate?
choices: $$\text{CaHCO}_3$$
$$\text{Ca}_2\text{HCO}_3$$
$$\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2$$
$$\text{CaCO}_3$$
questions.explanation: Balancing one $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ cation ($$+2$$) requires two $$-1$$ bicarbonate packages ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$), which must be enclosed in parentheses as $$\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2$$.

questions.prompt: In one formula unit of calcium bicarbonate, $$\text{Ca(HCO}_3)_2$$, how many total oxygen atoms and how many total hydrogen atoms are represented?
choices: 3 oxygen atoms and 1 hydrogen atom
6 oxygen atoms and 2 hydrogen atoms
5 oxygen atoms and 2 hydrogen atoms
6 oxygen atoms and 1 hydrogen atom
questions.explanation: The subscript $$2$$ outside the parentheses multiplies everything inside the $$\text{HCO}_3^-$$ group by $$2$$, giving $$2 \times 3 = 6$$ oxygen atoms and $$2 \times 1 = 2$$ hydrogen atoms.

chunks.title: Your Blood's Chemical Shock Absorber: Bicarbonate in Human Physiology
chunks.content_markdown:
The partnership between carbonate ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$) and bicarbonate ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$) isn't just for kitchen baking and tea kettles—it is keeping you alive right now with every breath you take. Your cells constantly produce carbon dioxide as they burn glucose for energy, and your blood plasma must stay within a razor-thin window of acidity for your proteins and heart muscle to work.

To guard that balance, your bloodstream circulates a generous supply of dissolved **bicarbonate ions** ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$) paired mostly with sodium cations ($$\text{Na}^+$$). Whenever hardworking muscles release extra acid ($$\text{H}^+$$ protons) into your blood, $$\text{HCO}_3^-$$ acts like a chemical sponge, catching an $$\text{H}^+$$ ion to become neutral $$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$$ (the gentle fizzy compound in seltzer water) so your blood never turns dangerously acidic. Next, in Section 6, we'll expand our polyatomic toolkit to three more everyday champions—sulfate, nitrate, and phosphate—and see how water molecules can tuck right inside a dry crystal!

questions.prompt: How does the bicarbonate ion ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$) in human blood plasma help protect the body when exercising muscles release excess $$\text{H}^+$$ ions?
choices: It splits into pure carbon metal and oxygen gas to cool down red blood cells
It converts sodium cations ($$\text{Na}^+$$) into divalent calcium cations ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$)
It precipitates out of the bloodstream as solid limestone crystals inside the veins
It catches excess $$\text{H}^+$$ ions to prevent dangerous spikes in blood acidity
questions.explanation: Dissolved bicarbonate ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$) serves as blood plasma's primary acid–base buffer, soaking up excess $$\text{H}^+$$ protons to keep blood acidity steady.

questions.prompt: Comparing the three carbon-oxygen species $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$ (carbonate), $$\text{HCO}_3^-$$ (bicarbonate), and neutral $$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$$, what happens each time one $$\text{H}^+$$ is added?
choices: The number of oxygen atoms increases by one while the charge stays -2
The central carbon atom is replaced by a positively charged sodium cation
The package breaks its covalent bonds and turns into monatomic carbide anions
The overall electrical charge steps up by +1, moving from -2 to -1 to 0
questions.explanation: Each added $$\text{H}^+$$ ion brings a $$+1$$ charge, shifting the package stepwise from divalent carbonate ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$, $$-2$$) to monovalent bicarbonate ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$, $$-1$$) to neutral $$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$$ ($$0$$).

sections.title: 6. Sulfate, Nitrate & Phosphate in Baths, Plants and DNA
sections.summary: Expands the learner's polyatomic fluency to the three great mineral oxyanions of bath salts, agriculture, and cellular life. Learners explore divalent sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$) in drywall gypsum ($$\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) and soothing Epsom bath salt (magnesium sulfate heptahydrate, $$\text{MgSO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$, gently decoding the raised hydrate dot as cozy water molecules crystallized into a solid lattice), monovalent nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$) in leafy spinach, beets, and soluble plant fertilizers like $$\text{KNO}_3$$ and $$\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$$, and trivalent phosphate ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$) alongside its protonated cousins ($$\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$$ and $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$) in DNA backbones, cellular ATP energy, and hard bone mineral calcium phosphate, $$\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$$.

chunks.title: Soothing Baths and Bedroom Walls: Meet Sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$)
chunks.content_markdown:
Pour a cup of soothing **Epsom salt** into a warm bath after a long hike, or tap your knuckles against the gypsum drywall of your living room, and you are meeting our next polyatomic star: the **sulfate ion**, $$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$. Inside a sulfate package, one central sulfur atom is covalently bonded to four surrounding oxygen atoms, and the entire five-atom cluster carries a double negative charge ($$-2$$).

Because sulfate is divalent ($$-2$$), it pairs effortlessly in a $$1:1$$ ratio with divalent alkaline earth cations like $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ and $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$:
- **Magnesium sulfate** ($$\text{MgSO}_4$$) is the active mineral in Epsom salt.
- **Calcium sulfate** ($$\text{CaSO}_4$$) is the mineral backbone of plaster of Paris, blackboard chalk, and drywall gypsum.
- Paired with monovalent sodium ($$\text{Na}^+$$), it takes *two* $$\text{Na}^+$$ cations to balance one $$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$ package, giving **sodium sulfate** ($$\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$$), a key helper in powdered laundry detergents.

questions.prompt: What is the exact atom count and overall electrical charge of a single sulfate polyatomic ion?
choices: One sulfur atom and three oxygen atoms carrying a -1 charge ($$\text{SO}_3^-$$)
One sulfur atom and four oxygen atoms carrying a -2 charge ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$)
Four sulfur atoms and one oxygen atom carrying a -2 charge ($$\text{S}_4\text{O}^{2-}$$)
One single monatomic sulfur atom carrying a -2 charge ($$\text{S}^{2-}$$)
questions.explanation: The sulfate ion ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$) consists of one central sulfur atom covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms, with an overall charge of $$-2$$.

questions.prompt: How can you distinguish the formula of 'sodium sulfide' from 'sodium sulfate' on a chemical label?
choices: Sodium sulfide is $$\text{Na}_2\text{S}$$ without oxygen, whereas sodium sulfate is $$\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$$ with four oxygens
Sodium sulfide is $$\text{NaSO}_4$$ with one sodium, whereas sodium sulfate is $$\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$$ with two sodiums
Sodium sulfide contains four oxygen atoms, whereas sodium sulfate contains no oxygen atoms at all
Sodium sulfide uses a Roman numeral in its name, whereas sodium sulfate uses Greek prefixes
questions.explanation: The '-ide' suffix in sodium sulfide indicates the single-element sulfide ion ($$\text{S}^{2-}$$, giving $$\text{Na}_2\text{S}$$), while '-ate' in sodium sulfate indicates the oxygen-rich polyatomic sulfate ion ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$, giving $$\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$$).

chunks.title: What Is That Raised Dot in $$\text{MgSO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$? Crystalline Hydrates
chunks.content_markdown:
If you look closely at the fine print on a pharmacy bag of Epsom salt, you won't just see $$\text{MgSO}_4$$—you will see the intriguing formula $$\text{MgSO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$! Those sparkly crystals in the bag feel completely dry between your fingers, so why is $$7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ written right inside the solid's formula, separated by a centered **raised dot** ($$\cdot$$)?

When certain ionic salts crystallize out of water, they tuck a fixed number of intact water molecules into regular pockets around the ions inside the solid crystal lattice. Chemists call such a water-hosting solid a **crystalline hydrate** (as opposed to the completely dry **anhydrous** salt, $$\text{MgSO}_4$$). In **hydrate dot notation**, the raised dot does *not* mean multiplication! Instead, $$\text{MgSO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$—named *magnesium sulfate heptahydrate*, using a Greek number prefix like *di-* ($$2$$), *penta-* ($$5$$), or *hepta-* ($$7$$) before *-hydrate*—means that for every $$1$$ formula unit of $$\text{MgSO}_4$$, exactly $$7$$ intact $$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ molecules are locked dryly inside the crystal.

questions.prompt: In the chemical formula for Epsom salt, $$\text{MgSO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$, what does the centered dot ($$\cdot$$) followed by $$7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ mean?
choices: The magnesium sulfate must be multiplied by 7 before dissolving it in bathwater
The salt exists only as a liquid puddle containing 7 parts water to 1 part magnesium
Seven hydrogen ions have permanently replaced the magnesium cation inside the sulfate ion
Each $$\text{MgSO}_4$$ unit has 7 intact water molecules tucked into its solid crystal lattice
questions.explanation: In a crystalline hydrate, the centered dot indicates that a fixed whole number of intact water molecules (here, $$7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) are incorporated into the solid crystal structure per formula unit of salt.

questions.prompt: Drywall gypsum is calcium sulfate dihydrate, $$\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$. Counting both the $$\text{CaSO}_4$$ unit and its two water molecules, how many total oxygen atoms are in one hydrated unit?
choices: 4 total oxygen atoms
5 total oxygen atoms
6 total oxygen atoms
8 total oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: There are $$4$$ oxygen atoms inside the $$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$ ion plus $$1$$ oxygen atom inside each of the $$2$$ water molecules ($$2 \times 1 = 2$$), giving $$4 + 2 = 6$$ oxygen atoms total.

chunks.title: Feeding Beets, Spinach & Garden Soils: Meet Nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$)
chunks.content_markdown:
Every leafy green spinach leaf, roasted red beet, and backyard tomato plant depends on nitrogen to build its proteins and green chlorophyll. Yet plants cannot sip the unreactive diatomic nitrogen gas ($$\text{N}_2$$) floating in the air around them! Instead, plant roots drink nitrogen from soil water chiefly in the form of the **nitrate ion**, $$\text{NO}_3^-$$.

A **nitrate** package consists of one central nitrogen atom covalently bonded to three oxygen atoms, carrying a single negative charge ($$-1$$). Notice the difference in charge between carbonate ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$, charge $$-2$$) and nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$, charge $$-1$$): even though both have three oxygens, nitrate is monovalent! That allows nitrate to form extraordinarily water-soluble salts:
- **Potassium nitrate** ($$\text{KNO}_3$$) pairs one $$\text{K}^+$$ with one $$\text{NO}_3^-$$.
- **Calcium nitrate** ($$\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2$$) pairs one $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ with two $$\text{NO}_3^-$$ packages.
- **Ammonium nitrate** ($$\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$$) pairs two polyatomic ions—one $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ and one $$\text{NO}_3^-$$—in a double-nitrogen fertilizer!

questions.prompt: Even though both carbonate ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$) and nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$) contain three oxygen atoms, how do their formulas with calcium ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$) compare?
choices: Both form 1:1 formulas without parentheses: $$\text{CaCO}_3$$ and $$\text{CaNO}_3$$
Calcium carbonate is $$\text{CaCO}_3$$, whereas calcium nitrate requires two -1 packages as $$\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2$$
Calcium carbonate requires parentheses as $$\text{Ca(CO}_3)_2$$, whereas calcium nitrate is $$\text{CaNO}_3$$
Neither ion can bond with calcium because oxygen-containing ions repel alkaline earth metals
questions.explanation: Because carbonate carries a $$-2$$ charge ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$), one package balances $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ in $$\text{CaCO}_3$$; because nitrate carries only a $$-1$$ charge ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$), two packages are needed to balance $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ in $$\text{Ca(NO}_3)_2$$.

questions.prompt: High-nitrogen garden fertilizer often contains ammonium nitrate, $$\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$$. Why can this ionic salt exist without any metal atoms at all?
choices: Because it pairs a polyatomic cation ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$) with a polyatomic anion ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$)
Because nitrogen acts as a transition metal whenever it is surrounded by hydrogen
Because $$\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$$ is a noble gas rather than a crystalline ionic solid
Because oxygen carries a +2 positive charge that replaces the need for a metal cation
questions.explanation: An ionic compound simply requires positive cations and negative anions; in $$\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$$, the positively charged ammonium package ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$) balances the negatively charged nitrate package ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$) $$1:1$$.

chunks.title: The Trivalent Heavyweight of Bones & DNA: Meet Phosphate ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$)
chunks.content_markdown:
If carbonate builds seashells, what mineral gives your own teeth and skeleton their rock-solid strength? Meet the trivalent champion of human biology: the **phosphate ion**, $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$. Inside a phosphate package, one central phosphorus atom is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms, and the five-atom cluster carries a triple negative charge ($$-3$$).

Look at how calcium ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$) and phosphate ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$) team up to build the mineral scaffolding of your bones and tooth enamel, **calcium phosphate**. To balance $$+2$$ cations with $$-3$$ anions, nature aims for a six-charge handshake: **three** $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ cations supply $$3 \times (+2) = +6$$, and **two** complete $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$ packages supply $$2 \times (-3) = -6$$. Wrapping the two phosphate packages in parentheses gives the unmistakable formula of bone mineral: $$\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$$!

questions.prompt: Hard bone mineral is largely calcium phosphate, $$\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$$. Why does this formula unit combine three $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ ions with two $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$ packages?
choices: Because each calcium ion must attach directly to four oxygen atoms to stay stable
Because phosphorus carries a +3 charge that repels more than two packages per crystal
Because subscripts in bone minerals must always add up to the atomic number of carbon
Because three +2 calcium ions and two -3 phosphate packages balance to zero net charge
questions.explanation: Each $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ ion contributes $$+2$$ (for $$3 \times +2 = +6$$) and each $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$ ion contributes $$-3$$ (for $$2 \times -3 = -6$$), achieving electrical neutrality at $$+6 + (-6) = 0$$.

questions.prompt: Looking inside one formula unit of calcium phosphate, $$\text{Ca}_3(\text{PO}_4)_2$$, how many phosphorus atoms and how many oxygen atoms are present?
choices: 1 phosphorus atom and 4 oxygen atoms
2 phosphorus atoms and 6 oxygen atoms
2 phosphorus atoms and 8 oxygen atoms
3 phosphorus atoms and 8 oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: The subscript $$2$$ outside the parentheses multiplies the entire $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$ package by $$2$$, yielding $$2 \times 1 = 2$$ phosphorus atoms and $$2 \times 4 = 8$$ oxygen atoms.

chunks.title: Phosphate's Protonated Cousins in Cells and Plant Food: $$\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$$ & $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$
chunks.content_markdown:
