Just as carbonate ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$) can catch a proton to become bicarbonate ($$\text{HCO}_3^-$$), trivalent **phosphate** ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$) can catch one or two $$\text{H}^+$$ protons in water, stepping its charge up by $$+1$$ each time:
- Catch **one** $$\text{H}^+$$: $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$ ($$-3$$) becomes **hydrogen phosphate**, $$\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$$ (charge $$-2$$).
- Catch **two** $$\text{H}^+$$ ions: it becomes **dihydrogen phosphate**, $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$ (charge $$-1$$).

Inside your cells, the reversible trading of $$\text{H}^+$$ between $$\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$$ and $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$ serves as the primary intracellular fluid buffer, while linked phosphate groups form the backbone of DNA and the three-phosphate energy spring of **ATP** (*adenosine triphosphate*). You have now met carbonate, sulfate, nitrate, and phosphate—and notice that every single one ends in `-ate`! What happens when an ingredient label lists sodium *nitrite* or sodium *sulfite* with an `-ite` ending instead? Section 7 reveals the clean family secret.

questions.prompt: Starting from the phosphate ion ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$), what happens to the ion's formula and net charge when it attaches two $$\text{H}^+$$ ions?
choices: It becomes $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$, with its net charge stepping from -3 up to -1
It becomes $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_2^{3-}$$, losing two oxygens while keeping its -3 charge
It becomes $$\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$$, with its net charge stepping from -3 down to -5
It becomes neutral $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4$$, with all electrical charge completely gone
questions.explanation: Adding two $$+1$$ hydrogen ions ($$\text{H}^+$$) to trivalent $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$ ($$-3$$) shifts the charge by $$+2$$, yielding the monovalent dihydrogen phosphate ion, $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$ (charge $$-1$$).

questions.prompt: Baking powders and plant fertilizers often use 'monopotassium phosphate' (potassium dihydrogen phosphate), pairing $$\text{K}^+$$ with $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$. What is its neutral formula?
choices: $$\text{K}_3\text{PO}_4$$
$$\text{K}_2\text{HPO}_4$$
$$\text{KH}_2\text{PO}_4$$
$$\text{K(H}_2\text{PO}_4)_3$$
questions.explanation: Because potassium is $$\text{K}^+$$ ($$+1$$) and dihydrogen phosphate is $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$ ($$-1$$), they balance in a $$1:1$$ ratio as $$\text{KH}_2\text{PO}_4$$.

sections.title: 7. Systematic '-ate' vs. '-ite' Oxyanion Logic
sections.summary: Replaces rote flashcard memorization with the clean, predictable naming pattern that governs oxygen-bearing polyatomic ions (oxyanions). Learners see that changing an oxyanion's suffix from '-ate' to '-ite' simply removes one oxygen atom while keeping the central atom and the overall ionic charge 100% identical—contrasting plant-feeding nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$) with cured-meat preservative nitrite ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$ in sodium nitrite, $$\text{NaNO}_2$$) and bath-salt sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$) with dried-fruit and wine antioxidant sulfite ($$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$ in sodium sulfite, $$\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3$$)—before taking a friendly household peek at 'hypo-' (even less oxygen) and 'per-' (one more oxygen) through laundry bleach sodium hypochlorite ($$\text{NaClO}$$, containing $$\text{ClO}^-$$) and perchlorate ($$\text{ClO}_4^-$$).

chunks.title: One Letter Apart on the Deli Label: What Is an Oxyanion?
chunks.content_markdown:
Stroll past the deli counter at the grocery store and read the curing ingredients on a package of smoky bacon or corned beef: alongside sea salt, you will almost always spot **sodium nitrite** and **sodium nitrate**. Only one vowel separates *-ate* from *-ite*, yet food safety rules measure them to the fraction of a milligram! What do those two suffixes actually mean?

First, notice what carbonate ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$), nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$), sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$), and phosphate ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$) all share: each consists of a nonmetal central atom surrounded by covalently bonded oxygen atoms. Chemists call any negatively charged polyatomic ion made of a central element bonded to oxygen an **oxyanion** (or *oxoanion*). Because several nonmetals—especially nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorus, and chlorine—can stably bond to *more than one* number of oxygen atoms, chemistry uses the suffixes `-ate` and `-ite` to tell the oxygen-rich sibling apart from the oxygen-lighter sibling.

questions.prompt: What do chemists mean when they classify a polyatomic ion such as nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$) or sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$) as an 'oxyanion'?
choices: It is a positively charged oxygen cation that has lost all of its valence electrons
It is a negatively charged polyatomic ion with a central atom covalently bonded to oxygen
It is a pure diatomic oxygen gas molecule dissolved inside a liquid metal
It is any monatomic anion formed from the halogen column of the periodic table
questions.explanation: An oxyanion is a polyatomic anion consisting of a central atom (usually a nonmetal like $$\text{C}$$, $$\text{N}$$, $$\text{S}$$, $$\text{P}$$, or $$\text{Cl}$$) covalently bonded to one or more oxygen atoms.

questions.prompt: Why does chemical nomenclature need two different suffixes ('-ate' and '-ite') for oxyanions of the same central element?
choices: Because the central nonmetal can bond to different counts of oxygen atoms
Because the suffix changes from '-ate' to '-ite' whenever the ion dissolves in water
Because '-ate' is used for solid crystals and '-ite' is used only for hot vapors
Because '-ate' names the positive cation and '-ite' names the negative anion
questions.explanation: Many nonmetals form a pair of common oxyanions that differ in how many oxygen atoms surround the central atom; '-ate' names the more oxygen-rich ion and '-ite' names the ion with one fewer oxygen.

chunks.title: The Golden Family Rule: '-ite' Means One Less Oxygen, Same Exact Charge!
chunks.content_markdown:
Here is the golden rule that saves you from ever memorizing dozens of separate flashcards: **the `-ate` vs. `-ite` oxygen-count rule**.

Once you know the formula and charge of an element's standard `-ate` oxyanion, its `-ite` sibling always has:
1. **Exactly one fewer oxygen atom**, AND
2. **The exact same overall electrical charge!**

Never change the charge when stepping from `-ate` to `-ite`! Why doesn't the charge change? Because the extra or missing oxygen atom joins the covalent cluster as a neutral six-valence-electron partner, leaving the net electron surplus on the package untouched. So if you know **nitrate** is $$\text{NO}_3^-$$ (three oxygens, charge $$-1$$), you immediately know **nitrite** is $$\text{NO}_2^-$$ (two oxygens, still charge $$-1$$). And if **sulfate** is $$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$ (four oxygens, charge $$-2$$), then **sulfite** is automatically $$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$ (three oxygens, still charge $$-2$$)!

questions.prompt: According to the systematic '-ate' vs. '-ite' rule, how does an '-ite' oxyanion compare to the corresponding '-ate' oxyanion of the same central element?
choices: It has one fewer oxygen atom and the exact same overall electrical charge
It has the exact same number of oxygen atoms but one less negative charge
It has two fewer oxygen atoms and flips its charge from negative to positive
It replaces all of its oxygen atoms with hydrogen atoms of the same charge
questions.explanation: Stepping from an '-ate' oxyanion to its '-ite' partner always removes exactly one oxygen atom while keeping the central atom and overall ionic charge unchanged.

questions.prompt: You already know that the phosphate ion has the formula $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$. Applying the '-ate' to '-ite' rule, what is the formula and charge of the phosphite ion?
questions.explanation: Removing one oxygen atom from phosphate ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$) while keeping the exact same $$-3$$ charge gives phosphite, $$\text{PO}_3^{3-}$$.

chunks.title: Curing Bacon & Preserving Dried Apricots: Nitrite ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$) and Sulfite ($$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$)
chunks.content_markdown:
Let's watch **nitrite** ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$) and **sulfite** ($$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$) at work in your kitchen—and see how their formulas with sodium practically write themselves.

In traditional meat curing, a tiny pinch of **sodium nitrite** pairs one $$\text{Na}^+$$ cation ($$+1$$) with one nitrite package ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$, $$-1$$) to give $$\text{NaNO}_2$$. That missing third oxygen makes nitrite far more reactive than nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$), allowing $$\text{NaNO}_2$$ to block deadly *Clostridium botulinum* bacteria and give cured ham and pastrami their signature pink color.

Meanwhile, on bags of golden dried apricots and bottles of vintage wine, you will read "Contains **sulfites**"—often added as **sodium sulfite**. Since sulfite ($$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$) keeps the exact same $$-2$$ charge as sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$), it takes *two* $$\text{Na}^+$$ ions to balance one $$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$ package, giving $$\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3$$! Because $$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$ eagerly grabs stray oxygen before it can brown fruit or spoil wine, it acts as a gentle culinary antioxidant.

questions.prompt: Sodium nitrite is used in tiny regulated amounts to prevent botulism in cured meats. Given that sodium is $$\text{Na}^+$$ and nitrate is $$\text{NO}_3^-$$, what is the formula of sodium nitrite?
choices: $$\text{NaNO}_3$$
$$\text{NaNO}_2$$
$$\text{Na}_2\text{NO}_2$$
$$\text{Na}_3\text{N}$$
questions.explanation: Nitrite has one fewer oxygen than nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$) with the same $$-1$$ charge, giving $$\text{NO}_2^-$$; paired $$1:1$$ with $$\text{Na}^+$$, the formula is $$\text{NaNO}_2$$.

questions.prompt: Winemakers use sodium sulfite as an antioxidant preservative. Given that sulfate is $$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$, what is the neutral chemical formula for sodium sulfite?
choices: $$\text{NaSO}_3$$
$$\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$$
$$\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3$$
$$\text{Na}_2\text{S}$$
questions.explanation: Sulfite has one fewer oxygen than sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$) and keeps the $$-2$$ charge ($$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$), requiring two $$\text{Na}^+$$ cations to form $$\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3$$.

chunks.title: Laundry Bleach & Four Steps of Oxygen: 'Hypo-' and 'Per-' Oxyanions
chunks.content_markdown:
What if a resourceful nonmetal like chlorine can hold onto *four* different counts of oxygen atoms—1, 2, 3, or 4—all carrying a $$-1$$ charge? Two suffixes (`-ate` and `-ite`) cover the middle two steps, so chemists add two intuitive Greek prefixes for the bottom and top rungs of the ladder:
- **Per-...-ate** (*per-* from "hyper," meaning *one more* oxygen than `-ate`): **perchlorate**, $$\text{ClO}_4^-$$.
- **...-ate** (the reference rung): **chlorate**, $$\text{ClO}_3^-$$.
- **...-ite** (one fewer oxygen than `-ate`): **chlorite**, $$\text{ClO}_2^-$$.
- **Hypo-...-ite** (*hypo-* meaning *under*, or one fewer oxygen than `-ite`): **hypochlorite**, $$\text{ClO}^-$$.

Look at that bottom rung: **hypochlorite**, $$\text{ClO}^-$$! Pair one $$\text{Na}^+$$ ion with one $$\text{ClO}^-$$ ion and you get **sodium hypochlorite** ($$\text{NaClO}$$ or $$\text{NaOCl}$$)—the active whitening and disinfecting ingredient in every bottle of liquid household laundry bleach!

questions.prompt: Liquid household bleach is an aqueous solution of sodium hypochlorite, $$\text{NaClO}$$. How does the hypochlorite ion ($$\text{ClO}^-$$) relate to the chlorate ion ($$\text{ClO}_3^-$$)?
choices: It has two more oxygen atoms than chlorate and carries a -3 charge
It replaces all oxygen atoms with hydrogen atoms and carries a +1 charge
It is the monatomic chloride ion ($$\text{Cl}^-$$) with no oxygen atoms attached
It has two fewer oxygen atoms than chlorate while keeping the same -1 charge
questions.explanation: Stepping down from chlorate ($$\text{ClO}_3^-$$) by one oxygen gives chlorite ($$\text{ClO}_2^-$$), and stepping down one more oxygen ('hypo-...-ite') gives hypochlorite ($$\text{ClO}^-$$), all with a $$-1$$ charge.

questions.prompt: Given that chlorate is $$\text{ClO}_3^-$$, what does the prefix 'per-' in the perchlorate ion tell us about its formula and charge?
choices: It has one more oxygen atom than chlorate and keeps the -1 charge ($$\text{ClO}_4^-$$)
It has the same oxygen count as chlorate but doubles its charge to -2 ($$\text{ClO}_3^{2-}$$)
It has one fewer oxygen atom than chlorite and carries a +1 charge ($$\text{ClO}^+$$)
It contains two chlorine atoms bonded to a single oxygen atom ($$\text{Cl}_2\text{O}^-$$)
questions.explanation: In oxyanion naming, adding 'per-' to an '-ate' ion means one additional oxygen atom with the exact same charge, turning chlorate ($$\text{ClO}_3^-$$) into perchlorate ($$\text{ClO}_4^-$$).

chunks.title: The Three-Suffix Compass: '-ide', '-ate', and '-ite' at a Glance
chunks.content_markdown:
Take a step back and admire how much chemical territory you can now navigate just by listening to the last three letters of an anion's name:
- **`-ide`** (like *chloride* $$\text{Cl}^-$$, *sulfide* $$\text{S}^{2-}$$, *nitride* $$\text{N}^{3-}$$) almost always means a **single-element monatomic anion** with *zero* oxygen atoms (with our friendly two-atom friend *hydroxide*, $$\text{OH}^-$$, as the key everyday exception).
- **`-ate`** (like *nitrate* $$\text{NO}_3^-$$, *sulfate* $$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$, *carbonate* $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$, *phosphate* $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$) signals the **standard oxygen-rich polyatomic oxyanion**.
- **`-ite`** (like *nitrite* $$\text{NO}_2^-$$, *sulfite* $$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$, *chlorite* $$\text{ClO}_2^-$$) signals an oxyanion with **one fewer oxygen atom than `-ate`** and the **exact same charge**.

Up to this point, every compound we have named has contained ions. What happens when two nonmetals—like carbon and oxygen, or nitrogen and oxygen—share electrons *without* forming ions at all? Section 8 reveals why Greek prefixes suddenly take center stage.

questions.prompt: Without looking up any table, what can you immediately conclude about the three potassium salts: potassium sulfide, potassium sulfite, and potassium sulfate?
choices: All three contain four oxygen atoms, but their charges are -1, -2, and -3 respectively
Sulfide has four oxygens, sulfite has three oxygens, and sulfate has no oxygen at all
Only potassium sulfide is an ionic salt, while sulfite and sulfate are uncharged gases
Sulfide has no oxygen, sulfite has three oxygens, and sulfate has four oxygens
questions.explanation: The '-ide' suffix indicates monatomic sulfide ($$\text{S}^{2-}$$ with no oxygen), '-ate' indicates standard sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$), and '-ite' indicates sulfite with one fewer oxygen and the same charge ($$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$).

questions.prompt: Calcium hypochlorite is sold as dry swimming-pool shock granules. Since calcium is $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ and hypochlorite is $$\text{ClO}^-$$, what is its neutral chemical formula?
choices: $$\text{CaClO}$$
$$\text{Ca(ClO)}_2$$
$$\text{CaCl}_2$$
$$\text{Ca(ClO}_3)_2$$
questions.explanation: Balancing one divalent $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ cation ($$+2$$) requires two monovalent hypochlorite packages ($$\text{ClO}^-$$, charge $$-1$$), wrapped in parentheses as $$\text{Ca(ClO)}_2$$.

sections.title: 8. Covalent Greek Prefixes & Life-Saving Name Precision
sections.summary: Explains why two nonmetals sharing electrons can combine in several distinct ratios without fixed ionic charges to lock them into a single partnership, making explicit Greek counting prefixes ('mono-', 'di-', 'tri-', 'tetra-', 'penta-', with leading 'mono-' omitted on the first element) essential in covalent naming. Learners vividly contrast sparkling-water carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$) with silent, lethal carbon monoxide ($$\text{CO}$$), compare dental laughing gas dinitrogen monoxide ($$\text{N}_2\text{O}$$) with reddish-brown urban smog nitrogen dioxide ($$\text{NO}_2$$) and phosphorus trichloride ($$\text{PCl}_3$$) vs. pentachloride ($$\text{PCl}_5$$), and cement the golden boundary rule: why covalent $$\text{CO}_2$$ and $$\text{SiO}_2$$ use Greek prefixes while fixed-charge ionic $$\text{CaCl}_2$$ and $$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$ never do.

chunks.title: Sparkling Water vs. the Smoke Detector Alarm: Why $$\text{CO}_2$$ and $$\text{CO}$$ Need Prefixes
chunks.content_markdown:
When a metal and a nonmetal form an ionic salt like $$\text{CaCl}_2$$, their fixed ionic charges ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ and $$\text{Cl}^-$$) allow only one neutral ratio, so we simply call it *calcium chloride*. But what happens when **two nonmetals** bond by sharing valence electrons to form a **binary covalent (molecular) compound**? Because nonmetals share electrons flexibly rather than trading fixed ionic charges, the same two nonmetal elements can often combine in several completely different molecular ratios!

Take carbon and oxygen. When a campfire or gas stove burns with plenty of fresh air, each carbon atom shares electrons with *two* oxygen atoms to form **carbon dioxide**, $$\text{CO}_2$$—the harmless bubbly gas in sparkling water and exhaled breath. Starve that flame of oxygen, however, and carbon shares with just *one* oxygen atom to form **carbon monoxide**, $$\text{CO}$$—an odorless, colorless gas that hijacks the iron(II) in your hemoglobin and is why every home needs a carbon monoxide detector.

questions.prompt: Why can't two nonmetals like carbon and oxygen be named simply 'carbon oxide' the way $$\text{CaO}$$ is named 'calcium oxide'?
choices: Because two nonmetals sharing electrons can combine in multiple stable ratios like $$\text{CO}$$ and $$\text{CO}_2$$
Because carbon and oxygen are variable-charge metals that require Roman numerals in parentheses
Because nonmetals cannot form chemical bonds unless at least three elements are present
Because oxygen loses its '-ide' suffix whenever it bonds with another nonmetal element
questions.explanation: Unlike fixed-charge ions ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ and $$\text{O}^{2-}$$), two nonmetals sharing electrons can form more than one discrete molecular compound (such as $$\text{CO}$$ and $$\text{CO}_2$$), requiring prefixes to specify the atom counts.

questions.prompt: Why is inhaling carbon monoxide ($$\text{CO}$$) from a poorly vented heater dangerous, even though exhaled carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$) is part of normal breathing?
choices: $$\text{CO}$$ is an ionic crystal lattice that precipitates inside the lungs as solid limestone
$$\text{CO}$$ contains a radioactive isotope of carbon that emits nuclear radiation in blood
$$\text{CO}$$ has three times as many oxygen atoms per molecule as normal carbon dioxide
$$\text{CO}$$ is a distinct molecule with one oxygen atom that binds tightly to hemoglobin's iron(II)
questions.explanation: As Dalton's Law of Multiple Proportions showed in Part I, changing the atomic ratio from $$\text{CO}_2$$ to $$\text{CO}$$ creates an entirely different molecule—one that latches onto hemoglobin's $$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$ sites and blocks oxygen transport.

chunks.title: Counting From One to Ten in Greek: The Prefix Rule (and the Quiet 'Mono-')
chunks.content_markdown:
To state the exact subscript count of each element in a **binary covalent compound**, chemists attach **Greek numerical prefixes** directly to the front of each element word, while still giving the second element the familiar `-ide` suffix:
- $$1 =$$ **mono-** | $$2 =$$ **di-** | $$3 =$$ **tri-** | $$4 =$$ **tetra-** | $$5 =$$ **penta-**
- $$6 =$$ **hexa-** | $$7 =$$ **hepta-** | $$8 =$$ **octa-** | $$9 =$$ **nona-** | $$10 =$$ **deca-**

Two small smoothing habits make these names roll naturally off the tongue:
1. **Never put `mono-` on the very first element!** If the first element has a count of $$1$$, we simply state its element name (we say *carbon dioxide* for $$\text{CO}_2$$, never "monocarbon dioxide"). On the *second* element, however, a count of $$1$$ **always** gets `mono-` (as in *carbon monoxide*, $$\text{CO}$$).
2. When `mono-`, `tetra-`, or `penta-` meets *oxide*, drop the awkward trailing `-o` or `-a` so you don't hiccup over double vowels (*monoxide* and *pentoxide*, not "monooxide").

questions.prompt: Why is $$\text{CO}_2$$ systematically named 'carbon dioxide' rather than 'monocarbon dioxide', while $$\text{CO}$$ is named 'carbon monoxide'?
choices: The prefix 'mono-' is omitted on the first element for a count of 1, but kept on the second element
Carbon in $$\text{CO}_2$$ actually contains two carbon atoms that overlap in the same spot
The prefix 'mono-' is only allowed on elements from the halogen family of the periodic table
The first element in a covalent formula never takes any Greek prefix, even for counts of 2 or 3
questions.explanation: By convention, a leading 'mono-' is omitted when there is only one atom of the first element (though prefixes for 2 or more, like 'di-', are always kept), whereas 'mono-' is explicitly included when there is one atom of the second element.

questions.prompt: Quartz sand and glass are made largely of the covalent network compound $$\text{SiO}_2$$ (silicon and oxygen). What is its systematic chemical name?
choices: Silicon oxide
Silicon(II) oxide
Silicon dioxide
Disilicon monoxide
questions.explanation: With one silicon atom (leading 'mono-' omitted) and two oxygen atoms ('di-' + 'oxide'), $$\text{SiO}_2$$ is systematically named silicon dioxide.

chunks.title: Laughing Gas vs. Brown City Smog: Reading $$\text{N}_2\text{O}$$, $$\text{NO}$$, and $$\text{NO}_2$$
chunks.content_markdown:
No pair of nonmetals shows off the power of Greek prefixes better than nitrogen and oxygen! When the first element has a subscript of $$2$$ or more, we *do* include its prefix right at the start of the name. Look at three famous nitrogen-oxygen molecules that couldn't be more different:

- **Dinitrogen monoxide** ($$\text{N}_2\text{O}$$): Two nitrogens (`di-`) and one oxygen (`mon-`). Commonly called *nitrous oxide*, this sweet-smelling gas is the gentle "laughing gas" dentists use for calm sedation—and the pressurized propellant that fluffs whipped cream out of a canister!
- **Nitrogen monoxide** ($$\text{NO}$$): One nitrogen and one oxygen. Commonly called *nitric oxide*, your own blood vessels make tiny puffs of $$\text{NO}$$ to relax arterial walls and lower blood pressure.
- **Nitrogen dioxide** ($$\text{NO}_2$$): One nitrogen and two oxygens (`di-`). A sharp, reddish-brown toxic gas from tailpipe exhaust that gives urban traffic smog its hazy brown tint.

questions.prompt: Dental 'laughing gas' (also used to whip cream in aerosol canisters) has the systematic name 'dinitrogen monoxide'. What is its molecular formula?
choices: $$\text{NO}_2$$
$$\text{N}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{NO}$$
$$\text{N}_2\text{O}_2$$
questions.explanation: 'Dinitrogen' indicates two nitrogen atoms ($$\text{N}_2$$) and 'monoxide' indicates one oxygen atom ($$\text{O}$$), giving the molecular formula $$\text{N}_2\text{O}$$.

questions.prompt: Be careful not to confuse neutral covalent molecules with charged polyatomic oxyanions! How does the smog gas $$\text{NO}_2$$ differ from the bacon-curing ion $$\text{NO}_2^-$$?
choices: $$\text{NO}_2$$ is a neutral gas named nitrogen dioxide, whereas $$\text{NO}_2^-$$ is a -1 ion named nitrite
$$\text{NO}_2$$ is an ionic salt named nitrite, whereas $$\text{NO}_2^-$$ is a gas named nitrogen dioxide
$$\text{NO}_2$$ contains two nitrogen atoms, whereas $$\text{NO}_2^-$$ contains two sodium atoms
There is no difference; both formulas represent the exact same substance and name
questions.explanation: Uncharged $$\text{NO}_2$$ is a discrete covalent gas molecule named nitrogen dioxide, whereas $$\text{NO}_2^-$$ carries an extra electron (a $$-1$$ charge) and is the polyatomic nitrite oxyanion found in salts like $$\text{NaNO}_2$$.

chunks.title: Tri-, Tetra-, and Penta- in Action: From Dry-Cleaning Solvents to Matches
chunks.content_markdown:
What happens when a molecule packs three, four, or five nonmetal atoms around a central partner? Our Greek prefixes handle them effortlessly:

- **Sulfur trioxide** ($$\text{SO}_3$$): One sulfur and three oxygens (`tri-`). When volcanic plumes or coal smoke release **sulfur dioxide** ($$\text{SO}_2$$), it can react with air to form $$\text{SO}_3$$, the precursor to acid rain. (Notice again: uncharged $$\text{SO}_3$$ is *sulfur trioxide* gas, whereas charged $$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$ is the *sulfite* ion!)
- **Carbon tetrachloride** ($$\text{CCl}_4$$): One carbon surrounded by four chlorine atoms (`tetra-`), a classic non-flammable solvent once used in dry cleaning and vintage fire extinguishers.
- **Phosphorus trichloride** ($$\text{PCl}_3$$) vs. **phosphorus pentachloride** ($$\text{PCl}_5$$): Because phosphorus sits in the third row of the periodic table, it can share electrons with either three chlorines (`tri-`) or five chlorines (`penta-`), while matchstick tips use **diphosphorus pentoxide** ($$\text{P}_2\text{O}_5$$) derivatives.

questions.prompt: What are the correct systematic names for the two binary covalent phosphorus compounds $$\text{PCl}_3$$ and $$\text{PCl}_5$$?
choices: Phosphorus(III) chloride and phosphorus(V) chloride
Phosphorus trichloride and phosphorus pentachloride
Monophosphorus chlorate and monophosphorus perchlorate
Triphosphorus monochloride and pentaphosphorus monochloride
questions.explanation: Because both phosphorus and chlorine are nonmetals, we use Greek numerical prefixes: 'tri-' for three chlorines in $$\text{PCl}_3$$ (phosphorus trichloride) and 'penta-' for five chlorines in $$\text{PCl}_5$$ (phosphorus pentachloride).

questions.prompt: A high-voltage electrical insulator gas has the systematic name 'sulfur hexafluoride'. Given that 'hexa-' means 6, what is its molecular formula?
choices: $$\text{S}_6\text{F}$$
$$\text{SF}_5$$
$$\text{SF}_6$$
$$\text{S}_2\text{F}_6$$
questions.explanation: 'Sulfur' (with no prefix) indicates one sulfur atom ($$\text{S}$$) and 'hexafluoride' indicates six fluorine atoms ($$\text{F}_6$$), giving the molecular formula $$\text{SF}_6$$.

chunks.title: The Golden Naming Boundary: Why $$\text{CO}_2$$ Gets 'Di-' and $$\text{CaCl}_2$$ Never Does
chunks.content_markdown:
You have now mastered both ionic naming and covalent naming—and here is the single checkpoint that keeps them from ever getting tangled: **look at the very first element in the formula before choosing your naming rule!**

- **Starts with a METAL (or $$\text{NH}_4^+$$)? -> IONIC RULE.** Charge balance already fixes the ratio, so **NEVER use Greek prefixes** (`mono-`, `di-`, `tri-`) on the ions! $$\text{CaCl}_2$$ is *calcium chloride* (never "calcium dichloride"), $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$$ is *aluminum oxide* (never "dialuminum trioxide"), and if the metal has variable charge, use a Roman numeral ($$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$$ is *iron(III) oxide*).
- **Built of TWO NONMETALS? -> COVALENT PREFIX RULE.** Because shared electrons allow multiple ratios, **ALWAYS use Greek prefixes** (`mono-`, `di-`, `tri-`, `tetra-`, `penta-`). $$\text{CO}_2$$ is *carbon dioxide* and $$\text{N}_2\text{O}$$ is *dinitrogen monoxide*.

Wait—what if the first element is **hydrogen** ($$\text{H}$$) paired with an anion in water, like $$\text{HCl}$$ or $$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$? That brings us to the delicious world of everyday acids in Section 9!

questions.prompt: Why is $$\text{NO}_2$$ named 'nitrogen dioxide' with the prefix 'di-', whereas sidewalk de-icing salt $$\text{CaCl}_2$$ is named simply 'calcium chloride' without 'di-'?
choices: Chlorine is a noble gas that cannot accept Greek prefixes in any chemical formula
Calcium has an atomic number of 20, which automatically replaces all Greek prefixes
Greek prefixes are only permitted when the second element in the formula is oxygen
$$\text{NO}_2$$ pairs nonmetals in multiple ratios, while $$\text{CaCl}_2$$ pairs fixed-charge ions
questions.explanation: Two nonmetals ($$\text{N}$$ and $$\text{O}$$) share electrons in multiple possible ratios and require Greek prefixes, whereas an ionic salt with a fixed-charge metal ($$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ and $$\text{Cl}^-$$) can only balance in one neutral ratio.

questions.prompt: Which of the following four compound names correctly follows the boundary rule between ionic naming and covalent naming?
choices: Magnesium dihydroxide for $$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$
Dialuminum trioxide for $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$$
Dinitrogen tetroxide for $$\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$$
Carbon(IV) oxide for $$\text{CO}_2$$
questions.explanation: $$\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$$ consists of two nonmetals, so it properly uses Greek prefixes as dinitrogen tetroxide; $$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$ and $$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$$ are fixed-charge ionic compounds that never use Greek prefixes.

sections.title: 9. Befriending Common Acids & Their Naming Bridge
sections.summary: Connects everyday kitchen, beverage, and household acids directly back to the anion names learners already know, treating acids intuitively as neutral hydrogen-paired packages that release $$\text{H}^+$$ ions in water. Learners trace the three clean naming bridges: binary '-ide' anions without oxygen become 'hydro-...-ic acids' (chloride $$\text{Cl}^-$$ to stomach hydrochloric acid, $$\text{HCl}$$), polyatomic '-ate' oxyanions become '-ic acids' (carbonate to seltzer's carbonic acid $$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$$, acetate to vinegar's acetic acid $$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$, sulfate to car-battery sulfuric acid $$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$, nitrate to nitric acid $$\text{HNO}_3$$, and phosphate to cola's tangy phosphoric acid $$\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$), and '-ite' oxyanions echo gently as '-ous acids' (nitrite to nitrous acid $$\text{HNO}_2$$ and sulfite to sulfurous acid $$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_3$$).

chunks.title: What Makes an Acid an Acid? Hydrogen-Balanced Anions in Water
chunks.content_markdown:
Squeeze a fresh lemon over grilled fish, splash apple-cider vinegar into a salad dressing, or take a sip of fizzy cola, and your taste buds immediately recognize the bright, crisp tang of an **acid**. In movies, "acid" is often caricatured as a glowing green liquid eating through steel floors, yet your kitchen pantry and your own body rely on gentle, life-essential acids every single day.

At the atomic level, what is an **acid**? Think of an acid as an electrically neutral compound in which **one or more negative anions are balanced by just enough positive hydrogen ions ($$\text{H}^+$$) to reach zero net charge**, ready to release (donate) those $$\text{H}^+$$ protons when dissolved in water. That is why almost every inorganic acid formula starts with $$\text{H}$$ on the left:
- A $$-1$$ anion (like $$\text{Cl}^-$$ or $$\text{NO}_3^-$$) pairs with **one** $$\text{H}^+$$ to make $$\text{HCl}$$ or $$\text{HNO}_3$$.
- A $$-2$$ anion (like $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$ or $$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$) pairs with **two** $$\text{H}^+$$ ions to make $$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$$ or $$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$.
- A $$-3$$ anion (like $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$) pairs with **three** $$\text{H}^+$$ ions to make $$\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$!

questions.prompt: Why does the chemical formula for sulfuric acid ($$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$) begin with two hydrogen atoms, whereas nitric acid ($$\text{HNO}_3$$) begins with only one?
choices: Because sulfate carries a -2 charge requiring two $$\text{H}^+$$ ions, while nitrate carries a -1 charge
Because sulfur is twice as heavy as nitrogen and pulls in twice as many neutral hydrogen gases
Because sulfuric acid is a solid ionic lattice whereas nitric acid is a noble gas
Because any acid containing four oxygen atoms must always begin with two hydrogens
questions.explanation: An acid formula balances the charge of its anion with $$+1$$ hydrogen ions ($$\text{H}^+$$): divalent sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$ , $$-2$$) needs two $$\text{H}^+$$ ions ($$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$), whereas monovalent nitrate ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$, $$-1$$) needs one ($$\text{HNO}_3$$).

questions.prompt: What characteristic behavior defines an acid when it is dissolved in liquid water?
choices: It absorbs all dissolved oxygen gas and turns the solution bright blue
It locks all cations and anions into an insoluble crystal precipitate at the bottom
It converts nonmetal atoms into transition metal cations carrying variable charges
It releases positively charged hydrogen ions ($$\text{H}^+$$ protons) into the water
questions.explanation: In water, an acid acts as a proton-donating compound, releasing positively charged hydrogen ions ($$\text{H}^+$$) and leaving behind its companion anion.

chunks.title: No Oxygen? Add 'Hydro-': Binary Acids & Your Stomach's $$\text{HCl}$$
chunks.content_markdown:
Because every acid is built from a familiar anion paired with $$\text{H}^+$$, **acid names come directly from the name of the anion inside them!** Let's start with the simplest case: a binary acid whose anion ends in **`-ide`** and contains **zero oxygen atoms**.

Whenever an oxygen-free `-ide` anion teams up with $$\text{H}^+$$ in water, we use **binary `hydro-...-ic` acid naming**:
> **`-ide` anion (no oxygen) $$\rightarrow$$ `hydro-` + [anion root] + `-ic acid`**

Take the chloride ion ($$\text{Cl}^-$$). Pair it with one $$\text{H}^+$$ in water and *chloride* becomes **hydrochloric acid**, $$\text{HCl}$$! Right now, the lining of your stomach maintains a pool of dilute **hydrochloric acid** ($$\text{HCl}$$) to unfold tough dietary proteins and sterilize stray microbes on your food. Similarly, fluoride ($$\text{F}^-$$) becomes glass-etching **hydrofluoric acid** ($$\text{HF}$$), and divalent sulfide ($$\text{S}^{2-}$$) with two $$\text{H}^+$$ ions becomes **hydrosulfuric acid** ($$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$).

questions.prompt: When does an acid's systematic name begin with the prefix 'hydro-' (as in hydrochloric acid, $$\text{HCl}$$)?
choices: Whenever the acid is dissolved in water, regardless of which anion it contains
Only when the acid is built from a simple '-ide' anion that contains no oxygen
Only when the acid contains four or more oxygen atoms surrounding a central nonmetal
Whenever the acid contains three hydrogen atoms at the front of its chemical formula
questions.explanation: The prefix 'hydro-' is reserved for acids built from `-ide` anions without oxygen (such as chloride $$\text{Cl}^-$$ $$\rightarrow$$ hydrochloric acid, $$\text{HCl}$$); oxygen-containing oxyacids never use 'hydro-'.

questions.prompt: When hydrogen bromide ($$\text{HBr}$$, containing the monatomic bromide ion $$\text{Br}^-$$) is dissolved in water to form an acid solution, what is its acid name?
choices: Bromic acid
Bromous acid
Hydrobromic acid
Perbromic acid
questions.explanation: Because bromide ($$\text{Br}^-$$) is a monatomic '-ide' anion with no oxygen, its aqueous acid follows the 'hydro-...-ic acid' rule to become hydrobromic acid.

chunks.title: From '-ate' to '-ic' (No 'Hydro-'!): Vinegar, Seltzer & Cola Acids
chunks.content_markdown:
What if the anion inside the acid *is* one of our oxygen-containing polyatomic **`-ate` oxyanions**? Chemists call any oxygen-containing acid an **oxoacid** (or *oxyacid*), and its naming bridge is even simpler—**drop `hydro-` completely and turn `-ate` into `-ic acid`**:
> **`-ate` oxyanion $$\rightarrow$$ [anion root] + `-ic acid`** *(a fun memory rhyme: "I **-ate** something **-ic**ky!")*

Look at the everyday staples waiting in your kitchen and garage that follow this exact bridge:
- **Carbonate** ($$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$ ) + $$2\text{ H}^+$$ $$\rightarrow$$ **carbonic acid** ($$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$$), the gentle tickle in seltzer water.
- **Acetate** ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$) + $$1\text{ H}^+$$ $$\rightarrow$$ **acetic acid** ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$ or $$\text{HC}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2$$), the sour heart of culinary vinegar.
- **Phosphate** ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$ ) + $$3\text{ H}^+$$ $$\rightarrow$$ **phosphoric acid** ($$\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$), the crisp tartness in dark cola sodas.
- **Sulfate** ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$ ) + $$2\text{ H}^+$$ $$\rightarrow$$ **sulfuric acid** ($$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$, in lead-acid car batteries), and **nitrate** ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$) + $$1\text{ H}^+$$ $$\rightarrow$$ **nitric acid** ($$\text{HNO}_3$$).

questions.prompt: Why does dark cola list 'phosphoric acid' ($$\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$) on its ingredient label rather than 'hydrophosphoric acid'?
choices: Because $$\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$ is built from the '-ate' oxyanion phosphate ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$) rather than an oxygen-free '-ide' ion
Because cola contains no liquid water for the hydrogen ions to dissolve into
Because phosphorus is a transition metal that drops prefixes when bonded to oxygen
Because 'hydro-' is only used when an acid has fewer than three hydrogen atoms
questions.explanation: Oxyanions ending in '-ate' (like phosphate, $$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$) form oxoacids named with '-ic acid' and never use the prefix 'hydro-', giving phosphoric acid for $$\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$.

questions.prompt: Kitchen vinegar is a dilute aqueous solution of acetic acid, often written as $$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$. When $$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$ donates its acidic $$\text{H}^+$$ proton in water, which polyatomic ion remains?
choices: The carbonate ion, $$\text{CO}_3^{2-}$$
The acetate ion, $$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$
The hydroxide ion, $$\text{OH}^-$$
The formate ion, $$\text{HCOO}^-$$
questions.explanation: Acetic acid ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$) is the '-ic' acid partner of the '-ate' ion acetate ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$); donating the terminal $$\text{H}^+$$ proton leaves behind $$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$.

chunks.title: The Gentle Echo: From '-ite' Oxyanions to '-ous' Acids
chunks.content_markdown:
To complete the acid naming bridge, what happens when we pair $$\text{H}^+$$ protons with one of our **`-ite` oxyanions** (the siblings that carry one fewer oxygen atom than `-ate`)? Again, we never use `hydro-`; instead, **`-ite` turns into `-ous acid`**:
> **`-ite` oxyanion $$\rightarrow$$ [anion root] + `-ous acid`**

Compare the `-ate`/`-ic` and `-ite`/`-ous` pairs side by side:
- **Nitrate** ($$\text{NO}_3^-$$) makes **nitric acid** ($$\text{HNO}_3$$) $$\leftrightarrow$$ **Nitrite** ($$\text{NO}_2^-$$) makes **nitrous acid** ($$\text{HNO}_2$$).
- **Sulfate** ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$) makes **sulfuric acid** ($$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$) $$\leftrightarrow$$ **Sulfite** ($$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$) makes **sulfurous acid** ($$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_3$$).
- **Chlorite** ($$\text{ClO}_2^-$$) makes **chlorous acid** ($$\text{HClO}_2$$), and **hypochlorite** ($$\text{ClO}^-$$) makes **hypochlorous acid** ($$\text{HClO}$$)—the gentle disinfecting sanitizer your own white blood cells produce to fight germs!

questions.prompt: When sulfur dioxide gas dissolves in rainwater, it forms the acid $$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_3$$, which contains the sulfite ion ($$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$). What is the systematic name of $$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_3$$?
choices: Sulfuric acid
Sulfurous acid
Hydrosulfuric acid
Hydrosulfurous acid
questions.explanation: Because the companion oxyanion in $$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_3$$ is sulfite ($$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$, ending in '-ite'), its oxoacid takes the '-ous acid' ending to become sulfurous acid.

questions.prompt: Human white blood cells generate $$\text{HClO}$$ to destroy invading bacteria, and $$\text{HClO}$$ is also sold as a gentle wound spray. Since $$\text{ClO}^-$$ is the 'hypochlorite' ion, what is $$\text{HClO}$$ named?
choices: Hydrochloric acid
Chloric acid
Hypochlorous acid
Perchloric acid
questions.explanation: Applying the '-ite' $$\rightarrow$$ '-ous acid' bridge directly to the hypochlorite ion ($$\text{ClO}^-$$) gives hypochlorous acid ($$\text{HClO}$$).

chunks.title: The Three-Bridge Acid Map: Sulfide, Sulfate, and Sulfite Side by Side
chunks.content_markdown:
Look at how cleanly the entire acid-naming system snaps into place when we line up the three sulfur anions side by side with their $$2\text{ H}^+$$ acid partners:

1. **Sulfide** ($$\text{S}^{2-}$$, ends in **`-ide`**, no oxygen) $$\rightarrow$$ **hydrosulfuric acid** ($$\text{H}_2\text{S}$$).
2. **Sulfate** ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$, ends in **`-ate`**, four oxygens) $$\rightarrow$$ **sulfuric acid** ($$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$).
3. **Sulfite** ($$\text{SO}_3^{2-}$$, ends in **`-ite`**, three oxygens) $$\rightarrow$$ **sulfurous acid** ($$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_3$$).

Notice how the prefix `hydro-` is your infallible detector for *no oxygen*: **hydrochloric acid** is $$\text{HCl}$$, whereas **chloric acid** (no `hydro-`!) comes from chlorate ($$\text{ClO}_3^-$$) and is $$\text{HClO}_3$$. You now hold every piece of the chemical naming puzzle—subscripts, parentheses, hydration dots, Roman numerals, polyatomic packages, Greek prefixes, and acid bridges. In Section 10, let's take a celebratory tour of real pantry and pharmacy labels!

questions.prompt: How do the chemical formulas of 'hydrochloric acid', 'chloric acid', and 'chlorous acid' differ from one another?
choices: Hydrochloric is $$\text{HClO}_4$$, chloric is $$\text{HClO}_3$$, and chlorous is $$\text{HCl}$$
All three have the formula $$\text{HCl}$$, but refer to solid, liquid, and gas states
Hydrochloric is $$\text{H}_3\text{Cl}$$, chloric is $$\text{H}_2\text{Cl}$$, and chlorous is $$\text{HCl}$$
Hydrochloric is $$\text{HCl}$$, chloric is $$\text{HClO}_3$$, and chlorous is $$\text{HClO}_2$$
questions.explanation: 'Hydro-...-ic' indicates the oxygen-free '-ide' anion chloride ($$\text{HCl}$$), '-ic' without 'hydro-' indicates the '-ate' oxyanion chlorate ($$\text{HClO}_3$$), and '-ous' indicates the '-ite' oxyanion chlorite ($$\text{HClO}_2$$).

questions.prompt: If a laboratory bottle is labeled 'nitrous acid', which chemical formula is inside the bottle?
choices: $$\text{HNO}_3$$
$$\text{HNO}_2$$
$$\text{H}_3\text{N}$$
$$\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$$
questions.explanation: The '-ous acid' ending points back to the '-ite' oxyanion—nitrite, $$\text{NO}_2^-$$—which pairs with one $$\text{H}^+$$ ion to form nitrous acid, $$\text{HNO}_2$$.

sections.title: 10. Everyday Pantry & Pharmacy Label Fluency
sections.summary: Brings the entire module together in a celebratory, confidence-building synthesis tour across real-world kitchen tins, toothpaste tubes, antacid bottles, fertilizer sacks, and oral-rehydration electrolyte packets. Learners practice a calm three-step diagnostic workflow—spotting whether a substance is a binary ionic salt, a polyatomic salt or hydrate, a covalent nonmetal pair, or an acid—while translating fluently between everyday common names (baking soda, washing soda, lye, milk of magnesia, limestone, Epsom salt, bleach, vinegar, laughing gas) and systematic chemical names and formulas, setting the stage for Part IV's balanced chemical equations.

chunks.title: Speaking Both Languages: Common Household Names vs. Systematic Names
chunks.content_markdown:
Congratulations—what used to look like intimidating Fine Print on the back of a grocery box or medicine bottle is now a language you can read fluently! In everyday life, many beloved substances wear two nametags at once: a traditional **trivial (common) name** handed down from cooking, mining, or apothecary history, and a **systematic IUPAC name** built from the exact rules we have explored.

Look at how many household classics you can now translate in a heartbeat:
- **Table salt**: sodium chloride ($$\text{NaCl}$$)
- **Baking soda**: sodium bicarbonate / sodium hydrogen carbonate ($$\text{NaHCO}_3$$)
- **Washing soda**: sodium carbonate ($$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$$)
- **Lye (caustic soda)**: sodium hydroxide ($$\text{NaOH}$$)
- **Milk of magnesia**: magnesium hydroxide ($$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$)
- **Chalk, limestone & Tums**: calcium carbonate ($$\text{CaCO}_3$$)
- **Epsom salt**: magnesium sulfate heptahydrate ($$\text{MgSO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$)
- **Liquid laundry bleach**: aqueous sodium hypochlorite ($$\text{NaClO}$$)
- **Vinegar's sour tang**: acetic acid ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$) | **Laughing gas**: dinitrogen monoxide ($$\text{N}_2\text{O}$$)

questions.prompt: A traditional soap-making recipe calls for 'lye,' while a laundry booster calls for 'washing soda.' Which pair of systematic names and formulas correctly matches these two common names?
choices: Lye is sodium hydroxide ($$\text{NaOH}$$), and washing soda is sodium carbonate ($$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$$)
Lye is sodium bicarbonate ($$\text{NaHCO}_3$$), and washing soda is sodium hypochlorite ($$\text{NaClO}$$)
Lye is calcium carbonate ($$\text{CaCO}_3$$), and washing soda is magnesium sulfate ($$\text{MgSO}_4$$)
Lye is hydrochloric acid ($$\text{HCl}$$), and washing soda is magnesium hydroxide ($$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$)
questions.explanation: Household lye (caustic soda) is systematically sodium hydroxide ($$\text{NaOH}$$), and laundry washing soda is sodium carbonate ($$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$$).

questions.prompt: Why do chemists and pharmacists maintain systematic IUPAC names alongside centuries-old common names like 'milk of magnesia' or 'Epsom salt'?
choices: Because a systematic name directly reveals the exact ions or atoms and their charge or count ratio
Because common names are only allowed for covalent gases and never for solid ionic salts
Because systematic names hide the identity of elements so competitors cannot copy recipes
Because common names change their chemical formulas depending on the season of the year
questions.explanation: While common names like 'Epsom salt' are convenient, systematic names like 'magnesium sulfate heptahydrate' let anyone reconstruct the exact chemical formula ($$\text{MgSO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$) from first principles.

chunks.title: The Medicine Cabinet Tour: Decoding Toothpaste Tubes & Antacid Bottles
chunks.content_markdown:
Flip over a tube of cavity-fighting toothpaste or a bottle of heartburn relief, and you will see ingredients divided into **active ingredients** (the specific compound delivering the therapeutic mineral or acid-neutralizing job) and **inactive ingredients** (the gentle abrasives, thickeners, and flavorings).

On a toothpaste tube, you might spot two different fluoride heroes under *Active Ingredient*: **sodium fluoride** ($$\text{NaF}$$) or **stannous fluoride**—which you now recognize as **tin(II) fluoride** ($$\text{SnF}_2$$), pairing one $$\text{Sn}^{2+}$$ cation with two $$\text{F}^-$$ anions! Down in the *Inactive Ingredients*, you'll see gentle polishing minerals like **calcium carbonate** ($$\text{CaCO}_3$$), **dicalcium phosphate dihydrate** ($$\text{CaHPO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$), and **hydrated silica** ($$\text{SiO}_2 \cdot n\text{H}_2\text{O}$$, built from covalent silicon dioxide).

Move to the antacid shelf and you meet **calcium carbonate** ($$\text{CaCO}_3$$), **magnesium hydroxide** ($$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$), and **aluminum hydroxide** ($$\text{Al(OH)}_3$$)—each carrying basic carbonate or hydroxide packages ready to neutralize excess stomach **hydrochloric acid** ($$\text{HCl}$$).

questions.prompt: A toothpaste tube lists 'stannous fluoride' (tin(II) fluoride, $$\text{SnF}_2$$) as its active ingredient and 'hydrated silica' (silicon dioxide, $$\text{SiO}_2$$) as its polishing abrasive. Why do their names follow different rules?
choices: $$\text{SnF}_2$$ is a covalent gas molecule, while $$\text{SiO}_2$$ is an acid that drops the prefix 'hydro-'
Both compounds are binary ionic salts, but fluorine never accepts Greek prefixes in any compound
$$\text{SnF}_2$$ is an ionic salt with a variable-charge metal, while $$\text{SiO}_2$$ pairs two nonmetals
Tin is a polyatomic oxyanion, whereas silicon is an alkali metal from the first column
questions.explanation: Tin(II) fluoride ($$\text{SnF}_2$$) pairs a variable-charge metal cation ($$\text{Sn}^{2+}$$) with fluoride anions (using a Stock Roman numeral), whereas silicon dioxide ($$\text{SiO}_2$$) combines nonmetals using the Greek prefix 'di-'.

questions.prompt: Extra-strength liquid antacids often combine magnesium hydroxide, $$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$, with aluminum hydroxide, $$\text{Al(OH)}_3$$. Why does aluminum require three hydroxide packages while magnesium requires two?
choices: Because hydroxide carries a -3 charge with magnesium and a -2 charge with aluminum
Because aluminum hydroxide is a crystalline trihydrate containing three water molecules
Because aluminum is a nonmetal that uses the Greek prefix 'tri-' to count its oxygens
Because aluminum forms a fixed $$\text{Al}^{3+}$$ cation, whereas magnesium forms a fixed $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ cation
questions.explanation: Each hydroxide package carries a $$-1$$ charge ($$\text{OH}^-$$); balancing divalent $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$ requires two $$\text{OH}^-$$ ions in $$\text{Mg(OH)}_2$$, while balancing trivalent $$\text{Al}^{3+}$$ requires three $$\text{OH}^-$$ ions in $$\text{Al(OH)}_3$$.

chunks.title: The Bakery & Potting Shed Tour: Double-Acting Powders and Plant Foods
chunks.content_markdown:
Now step into the kitchen bakery and out to the garden shed. Open a tin of **double-acting baking powder** and read the label: alongside **sodium bicarbonate** ($$\text{NaHCO}_3$$) and cornstarch (which keeps the powder dry), you will spot food-grade acid salts such as **monocalcium phosphate**—systematically **calcium dihydrogen phosphate**, $$\text{Ca(H}_2\text{PO}_4)_2$$! Look at all the pieces of your knowledge working together in $$\text{Ca(H}_2\text{PO}_4)_2$$: one $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ cation ($$+2$$) balanced by two monovalent dihydrogen phosphate packages ($$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$, charge $$-1$$ each), wrapped in parentheses.

Step out to the garden shed and read a bag of all-purpose N-P-K (Nitrogen-Phosphorus-Potassium) water-soluble plant food: you will see **ammonium phosphate**—$$\text{(NH}_4)_3\text{PO}_4$$, where *three* $$+1$$ ammonium packages balance *one* $$-3$$ phosphate package—alongside **potassium nitrate** ($$\text{KNO}_3$$), **ammonium sulfate** ($$\text{(NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$$), and trace mineral salts of **iron(II) sulfate** ($$\text{FeSO}_4$$) and **copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate** ($$\text{CuSO}_4 \cdot 5\text{H}_2\text{O}$$).

questions.prompt: Water-soluble garden fertilizers often supply both nitrogen and phosphorus using ammonium phosphate, $$\text{(NH}_4)_3\text{PO}_4$$. Why is the subscript outside the parentheses a 3?
choices: Because each individual ammonium ion contains three nitrogen atoms and twelve hydrogen atoms
Because phosphate carries a +3 charge that requires three -1 ammonia gas molecules
Because three +1 ammonium packages are needed to balance one -3 phosphate package
Because phosphorus is in the third row of the periodic table and requires a subscript of 3
questions.explanation: Each ammonium package carries a $$+1$$ charge ($$\text{NH}_4^+$$) and the phosphate package carries a $$-3$$ charge ($$\text{PO}_4^{3-}$$), so three $$\text{NH}_4^+$$ packages are needed to reach zero net charge.

questions.prompt: A lawn moss-control product lists 'ferrous sulfate heptahydrate' as its active ingredient. What is its systematic Stock name and chemical formula?
choices: Iron(III) sulfate heptahydrate, $$\text{Fe}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Iron(II) sulfite hexahydrate, $$\text{FeSO}_3 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Iron(II) sulfide heptahydrate, $$\text{FeS} \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Iron(II) sulfate heptahydrate, $$\text{FeSO}_4 \cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
questions.explanation: 'Ferrous' means iron(II) ($$\text{Fe}^{2+}$$), which balances divalent sulfate ($$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$) $$1:1$$ as $$\text{FeSO}_4$$, and 'heptahydrate' adds $$\cdot 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ for iron(II) sulfate heptahydrate.

chunks.title: Your Three-Step Diagnostic Compass: Any Formula to Any Name
chunks.content_markdown:
Whenever you meet an unfamiliar chemical formula or name in the wild, you never need to guess. Just walk calmly through this **three-step formula-to-name diagnostic workflow**:

1. **Step 1 — Check the First Partner**:
   - Is it a **metal** or **$$\text{NH}_4^+$$**? It's an **ionic compound** (never use Greek prefixes!).
   - Is it **two nonmetals**? It's a **binary covalent molecule** (use Greek prefixes `mono-`, `di-`, `tri-`, `tetra-`, `penta-`!).
   - Does it start with acidic **$$\text{H}$$** in water? Use the **acid naming bridge**!
2. **Step 2 — If Ionic, Check the Cation**:
   - Fixed-charge ($$\text{Na}^+$$, $$\text{K}^+$$, $$\text{Mg}^{2+}$$, $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$, $$\text{Al}^{3+}$$, $$\text{NH}_4^+$$)? Just say its name.
   - Variable-charge metal ($$\text{Fe}$$, $$\text{Cu}$$, $$\text{Sn}$$, $$\text{Pb}$$)? Deduce the ion's charge from the anion and write a **Roman numeral**!
3. **Step 3 — Check the Anion Ending**:
   - Single nonmetal (or $$\text{OH}^-$$) $$\rightarrow$$ **`-ide`**. Polyatomic oxyanion $$\rightarrow$$ **`-ate`** or **`-ite`** (one less oxygen, same charge).

questions.prompt: Using the three-step diagnostic workflow, what is the correct systematic name for the mineral supplement $$\text{CuSO}_4$$?
choices: Copper monosulfate
Copper(II) sulfate
Copper(I) sulfate
Cupric sulfite
questions.explanation: Step 1: Copper is a metal (ionic, no Greek prefixes). Step 2: Copper is variable-charge, and balancing one $$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$ ion ($$-2$$) means copper is $$\text{Cu}^{2+}$$ -> copper(II). Step 3: $$\text{SO}_4^{2-}$$ is sulfate -> copper(II) sulfate.

questions.prompt: Which of the following four formula-and-name pairs contains a naming error that violates our three-step diagnostic workflow?
choices: $$\text{KNO}_3$$ — potassium nitrate
$$\text{Ca(OH)}_2$$ — calcium dihydroxide
$$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$$ — iron(III) oxide
$$\text{SO}_2$$ — sulfur dioxide
questions.explanation: $$\text{Ca(OH)}_2$$ is an ionic compound with fixed-charge $$\text{Ca}^{2+}$$ and $$\text{OH}^-$$ ions, so it must be named simply calcium hydroxide—never with the covalent Greek prefix 'di-'.

chunks.title: Looking Ahead to Part IV: When Ingredients Meet & Rearrange!
chunks.content_markdown:
Look back at the journey you have completed across Parts I, II, and III. In Part I, you saw that matter is made of indestructible atoms combining in simple whole-number ratios. In Part II, you stepped inside those atoms to see how outer valence skins create positive cations and negative anions that power your nerves, heartbeats, and bones. And here in Part III, you learned to read and write the full language of chemistry—from crystal formula units and discrete molecules to Roman numerals, polyatomic team packages, hydration dots, Greek prefixes, and household acids.

Even better, you are now ready for the dynamic heart of chemistry in **Everyday Chemical Foundations IV**: what happens when two of our pantry heroes—say, baking soda ($$\text{NaHCO}_3$$) and vinegar's acetic acid ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$), or antacid calcium carbonate ($$\text{CaCO}_3$$) and stomach hydrochloric acid ($$\text{HCl}$$)—actually meet in the bowl and rearrange their partners into fizzing carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$) and water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$)? See you in Part IV!

questions.prompt: An oral rehydration electrolyte packet lists: sodium chloride ($$\text{NaCl}$$), potassium chloride ($$\text{KCl}$$), sodium bicarbonate ($$\text{NaHCO}_3$$), and anhydrous glucose ($$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$$). Which statement accurately describes these four ingredients?
choices: The first three are ionic salts that release electrolyte ions in water, while glucose is a discrete covalent molecule
All four ingredients are binary covalent gases that require Greek numerical prefixes in their systematic names
Only sodium bicarbonate contains ions, while $$\text{NaCl}$$ and $$\text{KCl}$$ are uncharged covalent molecules
Anhydrous glucose is a crystalline hydrate containing six intact water molecules per formula unit
questions.explanation: $$\text{NaCl}$$, $$\text{KCl}$$, and $$\text{NaHCO}_3$$ are ionic salts (two binary, one containing the polyatomic bicarbonate ion), whereas anhydrous glucose ($$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$$) is a water-free discrete covalent sugar molecule.

questions.prompt: When baking soda ($$\text{NaHCO}_3$$) reacts with vinegar's acetic acid ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$), it produces water ($$\text{H}_2\text{O}$$), carbon dioxide ($$\text{CO}_2$$), and dissolved $$\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$$. What is the systematic name of $$\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$$?
choices: Sodium carbonate
Sodium acetate
Acetic hydroxide
Monosodium monacetate
questions.explanation: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$$ pairs the sodium cation ($$\text{Na}^+$$) with the polyatomic acetate anion ($$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$$), giving the ionic salt sodium acetate.
